## 3. The floor, the ceiling, and the dyadic spectrum

**Theorem 3.1 (No starvation).** For every exchange and every class $y$,
$$\frac{\gamma\, d(y)}{\beta\log(1/p(y)) + M + \gamma - r(y)} \;\le\; \mathrm{service}(y).$$

*Proof.* The left side is $\mathrm{ideal}(y) > 0$; apply Lemma 2.1 with $\rho = 2$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.2 (Factor-two ceiling).** $\mathrm{service}(y) < 2\,\mathrm{ideal}(y)$ for every exchange and every class.

*Proof.* Lemma 2.2 with $\rho = 2$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.3.** $\mathrm{service}(y)/\mathrm{ideal}(y) \in [1,2)$ always.

**Theorem 3.4 (Exactness criterion).** $\mathrm{service}(y) = \mathrm{ideal}(y)$ iff $\mathrm{ideal}(y) = 2^k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

*Proof.* Lemma 2.4. $\square$

To show these constants are attained we need explicit exchanges. The following one-parameter family suffices.

**Definition 3.5 (Witness exchange).** For $x > 0$ let $W_x$ be the single-class exchange with $\beta = \gamma = M = 1$, $p \equiv 1$, $r \equiv 1$, $d \equiv x$.

Since $\log(1/1) = 0$, the gap of $W_x$ is $0 + 1 + 1 - 1 = 1$, hence $\mathrm{ideal}_{W_x} = \gamma x / 1 = x$. The witness family therefore realises *any* prescribed ideal share, and all questions about the slack spectrum reduce to questions about $\mathrm{gridCeil}$.

Combining with Lemma 2.3: if $1 < x \le 2$ then $\mathrm{service}_{W_x} = 2$, so the slack of $W_x$ is $2/x$.

**Theorem 3.6 (The slack spectrum is exactly $[1,2)$).**
$$\{\, c \in \mathbb{R} \;:\; \exists \text{ an exchange and a class with } \mathrm{service}(y) = c\cdot \mathrm{ideal}(y)\,\} \;=\; [1,2).$$

*Proof.* ($\subseteq$) Corollary 3.3. ($\supseteq$) Given $t \in [1,2)$, set $x = 2/t$. Then $x > 1$ because $t < 2$, and $x \le 2$ because $t \ge 1$. By Lemma 2.3, $\mathrm{service}_{W_x} = 2 = t \cdot (2/t) = t\cdot \mathrm{ideal}_{W_x}$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.7 (The floor is attained and optimal).** $W_1$ has $\mathrm{ideal} = 1 = 2^0$, so by Theorem 3.4 its service equals its ideal share exactly. Consequently no constant $c > 1$ satisfies $c\cdot\mathrm{ideal}(y) \le \mathrm{service}(y)$ for all exchanges.

**Corollary 3.8 (The ceiling is optimal).** For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an exchange with $(2-\varepsilon)\,\mathrm{ideal}(y) < \mathrm{service}(y)$; hence no constant $c < 2$ satisfies $\mathrm{service}(y) \le c\cdot\mathrm{ideal}(y)$ for all exchanges.

*Proof.* Take $x = 1 + \min(\varepsilon/4, 1/2)$, so $1 < x \le 2$ and $\mathrm{service}_{W_x} = 2$. One checks $(2-\varepsilon)x < 2$: if $\varepsilon \ge 2$ this is trivial, and if $\varepsilon < 2$ it is equivalent to $x - 1 < \varepsilon/(2-\varepsilon)$, which holds since $x - 1 \le \varepsilon/4 < \varepsilon/(2-\varepsilon)$ whenever $2 - \varepsilon < 4$. $\square$

Thus the mission statement — *the no-starvation constant cannot be improved beyond a factor of $2$* — holds in the strongest possible form: the bound $\mathrm{service} < 2\,\mathrm{ideal}$ is universal, the value $1$ is attained, and the value $2$ is the exact supremum.

## 4. Where the factor two comes from

The dyadic constants are not special. Replace the ladder $2^{\mathbb{Z}}$ by $\rho^{\mathbb{Z}}$.

**Theorem 4.1 (General grid, general witness).** For every $\rho > 1$ and every $t \in [1,\rho)$ there is an exchange with $\mathrm{service}_\rho(y) = t\cdot\mathrm{ideal}(y)$; namely $W_{\rho/t}$.

*Proof.* With $x = \rho/t$ we have $1 < x \le \rho$, so Lemma 2.3 gives $\mathrm{service}_\rho = \rho = t\cdot(\rho/t)$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.2 (Optimal ceiling constant).** For $\rho > 1$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$\big(\forall\ \text{exchanges}:\ \mathrm{service}_\rho(y) \le c\cdot\mathrm{ideal}(y)\big) \iff \rho \le c.$$

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) Lemma 2.2 gives $\mathrm{service}_\rho < \rho\,\mathrm{ideal} \le c\,\mathrm{ideal}$. ($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $c < \rho$. Put $t = \max(1, (c+\rho)/2)$; then $1 \le t < \rho$ and $c < t$. Theorem 4.1 supplies an exchange with slack exactly $t > c$, contradicting the bound. $\square$

**Theorem 4.3 (Optimal floor constant).** For $\rho > 1$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$\big(\forall\ \text{exchanges}:\ c\cdot\mathrm{ideal}(y) \le \mathrm{service}_\rho(y)\big) \iff c \le 1.$$

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) Lemma 2.1. ($\Rightarrow$) Theorem 4.1 with $t=1$ gives an exchange with $\mathrm{service}_\rho = \mathrm{ideal}$, forcing $c\cdot\mathrm{ideal} \le \mathrm{ideal}$ and hence $c \le 1$. $\square$

Specialising $\rho = 2$: $\mathrm{service} \le c\cdot\mathrm{ideal}$ holds universally iff $2 \le c$, and $c\cdot\mathrm{ideal} \le \mathrm{service}$ holds universally iff $c \le 1$. **The factor $2$ in the headline statement is precisely the grid ratio of the arbiter — nothing else.**

## 5. Aggregation and non-vacuity

**Theorem 5.1 (The floor aggregates).** For a finite family of classes, $\sum_y \mathrm{ideal}(y) \le \sum_y \mathrm{service}(y)$.

*Proof.* Sum Theorem 3.1 termwise. $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (The ceiling aggregates).** For a finite *nonempty* family, $\sum_y \mathrm{service}(y) < 2\sum_y \mathrm{ideal}(y)$.

*Proof.* Sum the strict inequality of Theorem 3.2 over a nonempty index set. $\square$

Quantisation costs the whole channel the same factor of two, no more. The bound is therefore an aggregate capacity statement, not just a per-class one.

**Theorem 5.3 (Rare channels are squeezed out).** For any $\varepsilon > 0$, if $\mathrm{gap}(y) > 2\gamma d(y)/\varepsilon$ then $\mathrm{service}(y) < \varepsilon$.

*Proof.* The hypothesis rearranges to $2\gamma d(y)/\mathrm{gap}(y) < \varepsilon$, i.e. $2\,\mathrm{ideal}(y) < \varepsilon$; combine with $\mathrm{service}(y) < 2\,\mathrm{ideal}(y)$. $\square$

Physically: as $p(y) \to 0$ the Boltzmann cost $\beta\log(1/p(y))$ diverges, the gap diverges, and the service tends to $0$. The floor of Theorem 3.1 is therefore a genuine, saturating constraint — a class *can* be driven to arbitrarily small service, and the floor is exactly the boundary of that decay.

## 6. Phase-jittered arbiters

A natural attempt to improve the worst case: randomise the ladder.

**Definition 6.1 (Jittered quantiser).** For $\rho > 1$, phase $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x > 0$,
$$J_{\rho,\theta}(x) \;=\; \rho^{\lceil \log_\rho x - \theta\rceil + \theta}.$$
For $\theta = 0$ this is $\mathrm{gridCeil}_\rho$; in general it is the ladder $\rho^{\mathbb{Z}}$ shifted multiplicatively by $\rho^{\theta}$.

**Theorem 6.2 (The guarantee is phase-independent).** For every $\rho>1$, every phase $\theta$ and every $x > 0$,
$$x \;\le\; J_{\rho,\theta}(x) \;<\; \rho\,x.$$

*Proof.* $\lceil t\rceil \ge t$ with $t = \log_\rho x - \theta$ gives $\lceil t\rceil + \theta \ge \log_\rho x$, hence the left inequality by monotonicity of $\rho^{(\cdot)}$. And $\lceil t\rceil < t+1$ gives $\lceil t\rceil + \theta < \log_\rho x + 1$, hence the right. $\square$

**Corollary 6.3 (Randomisation cannot help the worst case).** Since the two-sided bound of Theorem 6.2 is attained in the limit *at every fixed phase* — by Theorem 4.1 applied to the shifted ladder — no probability distribution over phases can lower the supremum of the slack below $\rho$, nor raise the infimum above $1$. The often-conjectured statement "randomisation improves the worst case" is **false** for this family.

What randomisation *does* change is the distribution of the slack, and that distribution is exactly computable.

**Theorem 6.4 (The log-slack is a circle rotation).** For $\rho > 1$, $x > 0$ and every phase $\theta$,
$$\log_\rho\!\Big(\frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\Big) \;=\; \{\theta - \log_\rho x\},$$
where $\{t\} = t - \lfloor t\rfloor$ is the fractional part.

*Proof.* $\log_\rho(J_{\rho,\theta}(x)/x) = \lceil \log_\rho x - \theta\rceil + \theta - \log_\rho x = \lceil u\rceil - u$ with $u = \log_\rho x - \theta$. The elementary identity $\lceil u\rceil - u = \{-u\}$ (verified separately for $u\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $u\notin\mathbb{Z}$) finishes the proof. $\square$

So as the phase $\theta$ sweeps a unit interval, the log-slack sweeps the circle $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ uniformly. The mean of the fractional part over any interval of unit length is $\tfrac12$, since $\{\cdot\}$ is $1$-periodic and $\int_0^1 t\,dt = \tfrac12$.

**Theorem 6.5 (Mean log-slack).** For every $\rho > 1$ and $x > 0$,
$$\int_0^1 \log_\rho\!\Big(\frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\Big)\,d\theta = \frac12, \qquad \int_0^1 \log\!\Big(\frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\Big)\,d\theta = \frac{\log\rho}{2}.$$

*Proof.* Substitute Theorem 6.4 and translate the integration variable: the integrand becomes $\{\theta - \log_\rho x\}$, an integral of a $1$-periodic function over a unit interval, hence equal to $\int_0^1\{t\}\,dt = \tfrac12$. Multiply by $\log\rho$ for the second identity. $\square$

**Theorem 6.6 (Geometric-mean slack).** For every $\rho > 1$ and every $x > 0$,
$$\exp\!\left(\int_0^1 \log\frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\,d\theta\right) \;=\; \sqrt{\rho}.$$

*Proof.* Immediate from Theorem 6.5: $\exp(\tfrac12\log\rho) = \rho^{1/2}$. $\square$

Note the striking uniformity: the typical slack does not depend on $x$ at all, hence not on the exchange. For the dyadic arbiter it is $\sqrt2 \approx 1.4142$, strictly below the worst case $2$.

**Theorem 6.7 (Arithmetic-mean slack).** For every $\rho > 1$ and every $x > 0$,
$$\int_0^1 \frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\,d\theta \;=\; \frac{\rho-1}{\log\rho}.$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 6.4 the integrand is $\rho^{\{\theta - \log_\rho x\}}$. Since $s \mapsto \rho^{\{s\}}$ is $1$-periodic, translating the variable reduces the integral to $\int_0^1 \rho^{s}\,ds$. Writing $\rho^s = e^{s\log\rho}$ and integrating gives $(\rho - 1)/\log\rho$. $\square$

For $\rho = 2$ this is $1/\log 2 \approx 1.4427$.

**Theorem 6.8 (Strict hierarchy of the three constants).** For every $\rho > 1$,
$$\sqrt\rho \;<\; \frac{\rho-1}{\log\rho} \;<\; \rho.$$

*Proof.* *Left inequality.* Set $u = \sqrt\rho > 1$, so $\log\rho = 2\log u$ and $\rho - 1 = u^2 - 1$. The claim becomes $u < (u^2-1)/(2\log u)$, i.e. $2\log u < u - 1/u$. Consider $f(u) = u - 1/u - 2\log u$ on $[1,\infty)$. Then $f(1) = 0$ and
$$f'(u) = 1 + \frac{1}{u^2} - \frac{2}{u} = \Big(1 - \frac1u\Big)^2 > 0 \quad (u>1),$$
a perfect square. Hence $f$ is strictly increasing on $[1,\infty)$ and $f(u) > 0$ for $u > 1$.

*Right inequality.* From $\log t < t - 1$ for $t > 0$, $t \ne 1$, applied with $t = 1/\rho$: $-\log\rho < 1/\rho - 1$, i.e. $\log \rho > 1 - 1/\rho = (\rho-1)/\rho$. Multiplying by $\rho/\log\rho > 0$ gives $\rho > (\rho-1)/\log\rho$. $\square$

For the dyadic arbiter: $1.4142\ldots < 1.4427\ldots < 2$.

**Interpretation.** Jitter does not change the *guarantee* — the floor and the ceiling are both exactly as before — but it converts the worst-case factor into a typical factor $\sqrt\rho$ and an average factor $(\rho-1)/\log\rho$. For capacity planning this is the practically relevant number; for admission control the worst case remains binding.

---

## 7. The optimal grid ratio

The grid ratio is a design parameter. A larger $\rho$ costs more in the worst case ($\mathrm{slack} < \rho$) but covers more logarithmic dynamic range per backoff level ($\log \rho$ per level). The natural figure of merit is therefore:

**Definition 7.1 (Grid cost).** $C(\rho) = \dfrac{\rho}{\log \rho}$ for $\rho > 1$: worst-case slack per unit of logarithmic range covered by one level.

**Theorem 7.2 (Euler's number is the unique optimum).** For every $\rho > 1$, $e \le C(\rho)$, with equality iff $\rho = e$; and $C(e) = e$.

*Proof.* Apply $\log t \le t - 1$ with $t = \rho/e > 0$: $\log\rho - 1 \le \rho/e - 1$, so $\log\rho \le \rho/e$, i.e. $e\log\rho \le \rho$, i.e. $e \le \rho/\log\rho = C(\rho)$ (using $\log\rho > 0$). Strictness: $\log t < t-1$ whenever $t \ne 1$, and $t = \rho/e = 1$ iff $\rho = e$. Finally $C(e) = e/\log e = e$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.3 (Binary and quaternary arbiters tie exactly).** $C(4) = C(2)$.

*Proof.* $\log 4 = 2\log 2$, so $C(4) = 4/(2\log2) = 2/\log 2 = C(2)$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.4 (The dyadic arbiter is within $7\%$ of optimal).** $C(2) < 1.07\, e$.

*Proof.* $C(2) = 2/\log 2$. Using $\log 2 > 0.6931471803$ and $e > 2.7182818283$ one has $2/\log 2 < 2.8854 < 1.07 \times 2.7182 < 1.07\,e$. $\square$

**Verdict (Theorem 7.5).** The dyadic arbiter satisfies, simultaneously: $e < C(2) < 1.07\,e$ (near-optimal grid design), worst-case slack exactly $2$ (unimprovable, Theorem 4.2), typical slack $\sqrt2 < 2$ (Theorem 6.6), and mean slack $1/\log 2$ strictly between them (Theorems 6.7, 6.8).

**A caution against over-claiming.** It is tempting to conclude that "the dyadic grid is optimal". This is *false*: $e$ is optimal, and $3$ is closer to $e$ than $2$ is ($C(3) = 3/\log 3 \approx 2.7307$ versus $C(2) \approx 2.8854$). The defensible statements are the quantitative $7\%$ bound and the exact tie $C(2) = C(4)$, which does explain why doubling the window is a natural fixed point of the design trade-off: over the integer ratios, the cost function is flat between $2$ and $4$ with a minimum at $3$ in between.

---

## 8. Diophantine dynamics: sharpness inside a single exchange

Everything so far quantifies over the space of exchanges. Sharpness meant: *some* configuration realises slack close to $2$. A sharper question, invisible at that level, is whether a **single running exchange** sees the whole spectrum over time.

Model the natural scenario: a class whose demand grows geometrically by a factor $\alpha > 0$ per round, so the ideal share runs along the ladder $\alpha^n$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. (By the witness family of Definition 3.5, every such ladder is realised by a genuine exchange, and $\mathrm{service}/\mathrm{ideal}$ for that exchange is exactly $\mathrm{slack}(\alpha^n)$.)

**Lemma 8.1 (Log-slack is a ceiling defect).** For $x > 0$, $\mathrm{logSlack}(x) = \{-\log_2 x\}$.

*Proof.* $\mathrm{slack}(x) = 2^{\lceil \log_2 x\rceil - \log_2 x}$, so $\mathrm{logSlack}(x) = \lceil u\rceil - u$ with $u = \log_2 x$, which equals $\{-u\}$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.2 (The demand ladder is a circle rotation).** For $\alpha > 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{Z}$,
$$\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^n) \;=\; \{\, n\cdot(-\log_2\alpha)\,\}.$$

*Proof.* $\log_2(\alpha^n) = n\log_2\alpha$; substitute into Lemma 8.1. $\square$

So the log-slack of the exchange, sampled round by round, is the orbit of $0$ under the rotation of the circle $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ by the angle $-\log_2\alpha$. The classical dichotomy for circle rotations now decides everything.

**Theorem 8.3 (Kronecker's theorem, in the form needed).** Let $\vartheta$ be irrational. For every $y \in (0,1)$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|\{n\vartheta\} - y| < \varepsilon$.

*Proof sketch.* The additive subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$ generated by $\vartheta$ and $1$ is dense precisely when $\vartheta \notin \mathbb{Q}$ (a closed subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$ is either cyclic or all of $\mathbb{R}$, and $\langle \vartheta,1\rangle$ cyclic would force $\vartheta$ rational). Choose $\delta = \min(\varepsilon, y, 1-y) > 0$ and pick a group element $z = m\vartheta + k$ with $|z - y| < \delta$. Then $0 < z < 1$, so $\{m\vartheta\} = \{z - k\} = \{z\} = z$, and $|\{m\vartheta\} - y| < \delta \le \varepsilon$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.4 (Dense slack orbit in the irrational case).** If $\alpha > 0$ and $\log_2 \alpha$ is irrational, then for every $s \in (0,1)$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^n) - s| < \varepsilon$. Consequently
$$[0,1] \;\subseteq\; \overline{\{\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^n) : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}}.$$

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 8.3 with $\vartheta = -\log_2\alpha$ (irrational since $\log_2\alpha$ is) and use Theorem 8.2. This shows the orbit closure contains $(0,1)$; taking closures again and using $\overline{(0,1)} = [0,1]$ together with idempotence of closure gives the display. $\square$

**Theorem 8.5 (A single exchange saturates both ends).** If $\log_2\alpha$ is irrational and $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, then
$$\exists\,n\in\mathbb{Z}:\ \mathrm{slack}(\alpha^n) > 2^{\,1-\varepsilon}, \qquad \exists\,m\in\mathbb{Z}:\ \mathrm{slack}(\alpha^m) < 2^{\,\varepsilon}.$$

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 8.4 with target $s = 1 - \varepsilon/2$ and tolerance $\varepsilon/4$ to obtain $n$ with $\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^n) > 1 - \tfrac34\varepsilon > 1-\varepsilon$; since $\mathrm{slack} = 2^{\mathrm{logSlack}}$ and $t\mapsto 2^t$ is increasing, the first claim follows. Symmetrically with target $s = \varepsilon/2$ and tolerance $\varepsilon/4$ for the second. $\square$

So one exchange, watched long enough, gets arbitrarily close to wasting a full factor of $2$, and on other rounds is served with essentially no waste at all.

**Theorem 8.6 (Periodicity and finiteness in the rational case).** Suppose $\log_2\alpha = p/q$ with $q \ne 0$ integers. Then for all $n,k\in\mathbb{Z}$,
$$\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^{\,n+kq}) = \mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^{\,n}).$$
If moreover $q > 0$, the orbit $\{\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^n) : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ is finite (of cardinality at most $q$), hence closed, hence *not* dense in $[0,1]$.

*Proof.* By Theorem 8.2, $\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^{n+kq}) = \{(n+kq)(-p/q)\} = \{n(-p/q) - kp\}$, and $\{t - j\} = \{t\}$ for integer $j$. For finiteness, every $n$ is congruent mod $q$ to some element of $\{0,\dots,q-1\}$, so the orbit is the image of a finite set. A finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed and cannot contain the infinite set $[0,1]$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.7 (Diophantine dichotomy).** For $\alpha > 0$,
$$[0,1] \subseteq \overline{\{\mathrm{logSlack}(\alpha^n) : n\in\mathbb{Z}\}} \iff \log_2\alpha \ \text{is irrational}.$$

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) Theorem 8.4. ($\Rightarrow$) If $\log_2\alpha = p/q$ is rational, write it with $q > 0$; Theorem 8.6 shows the orbit is finite and hence not dense. $\square$

**Sharpness for a fixed exchange is therefore a Diophantine property of the growth ratio, not a scheduling property.**

**Theorem 8.8 ($\log_2 3$ is irrational).** If $\log_2 3 = p/q$ with $p,q$ positive integers then $q\log 3 = p\log 2$, so $3^q = 2^p$ — impossible by unique factorisation (the left side is odd and exceeds $1$, the right side is even). Positivity of $p,q$ follows from $\log_2 3 > 0$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.9 (Ternary growth saturates the spectrum).** If demand grows by a factor $3$ per round, then $[0,1] \subseteq \overline{\{\mathrm{logSlack}(3^n)\}}$; quantitatively, for every $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ some round has slack exceeding $2^{1-\varepsilon}$ and some round has slack below $2^{\varepsilon}$.

*Proof.* Theorems 8.4, 8.5 and 8.8. $\square$

By contrast, growth ratio $\alpha = 4$ has $\log_2 4 = 2 \in \mathbb{Z}$, so every $\alpha^n$ lies on the dyadic grid and the slack is identically $1$: perfect efficiency forever. And $\alpha = \sqrt2$ has $\log_2\alpha = 1/2$, giving a period-$2$ orbit with slack values $\{1, \sqrt2\}$. The behaviour of a running exchange is decided entirely by the arithmetic of $\log_2\alpha$.

---

## 9. Algorithms

Three computational primitives summarise the theory.

**Algorithm 9.1 (Dyadic allocation).** Given $\beta,\gamma,M$ and per-class $(p,d,r)$, compute $\mathrm{gap} = \beta\log(1/p)+M+\gamma-r$; abort if $\mathrm{gap} \le 0$; compute $\mathrm{ideal} = \gamma d/\mathrm{gap}$; return $2^{\lceil\log_2\mathrm{ideal}\rceil}$. Cost: $O(1)$ per class, or $O(|\iota|)$ for the whole channel. Numerically, the ceiling must be computed carefully: when $\log_2\mathrm{ideal}$ is within floating-point epsilon of an integer, one should snap to that integer, otherwise a share that is exactly a power of two can be rounded to the *next* window and the reported slack jumps spuriously from $1$ to $2$.

**Algorithm 9.2 (Slack-orbit sampler).** Given a growth ratio $\alpha$ and a horizon $N$, return $\big(\{-n\log_2\alpha\}\big)_{n=0}^{N-1}$ together with the discrepancy of the sample against the uniform distribution. Cost $O(N)$ (or $O(N\log N)$ if the sample is sorted to compute the star discrepancy exactly). For irrational $\log_2\alpha$ the discrepancy tends to $0$; for rational $\log_2\alpha = p/q$ in lowest terms it stalls at a value bounded below by roughly $1/(2q)$, giving a practical numerical test of the dichotomy of Theorem 8.7.

**Algorithm 9.3 (Grid-cost optimiser).** Minimise $C(\rho) = \rho/\log\rho$ over $\rho > 1$. Since $C'(\rho) = (\log\rho - 1)/(\log\rho)^2$, the unique stationary point is $\rho = e$ and $C$ is strictly decreasing on $(1,e)$ and strictly increasing on $(e,\infty)$; a bisection on $C'$ or a direct golden-section search converges in $O(\log(1/\text{tol}))$ evaluations. Practically the routine is used to report the *relative excess* $C(\rho)/e - 1$ for a candidate ratio.

---

## 10. Applications and discussion

**Admission control.** Theorem 3.1 is the safety property a scheduler advertises. Theorem 4.2 says that the corresponding capacity reservation must be $\rho$ times the sum of ideal shares, and that this factor cannot be shaved: any admission controller that provisions less than $\rho\sum_y \mathrm{ideal}(y)$ can be defeated by an adversarial demand vector. Theorem 5.2 confirms the factor does not compound across classes.

**Capacity planning.** For *expected* throughput, the binding constant is not $\rho$ but $(\rho-1)/\log\rho$ (arithmetic mean, Theorem 6.7), or $\sqrt\rho$ if one is combining slacks multiplicatively across independent stages (geometric mean, Theorem 6.6). For $\rho = 2$ that is a planning factor of $1.44$ rather than $2$ — a $28\%$ difference in provisioned capacity, entirely accounted for by which mean is appropriate.

**Grid design.** Theorem 7.2 says a designer free to choose the ratio should choose $e$; Theorem 7.4 says $2$ costs at most $7\%$ more; Theorem 7.3 says $4$ costs exactly the same as $2$. Any protocol restricted to integer ratios and wanting the theoretical optimum should use $3$, at $C(3)\approx 2.7307$ versus the ideal $e \approx 2.7183$ — an excess of under half a percent.

**Diagnostics.** Section 8 has an operational reading. If a running class exhibits a slack that is constant, or cycles through a short finite list, its demand growth ratio is a rational power of the grid ratio, and the deployment is either perfectly efficient (slack $1$) or persistently wasteful by a fixed factor. If the observed slack wanders densely over $[1,2)$, the growth ratio is Diophantine-generic. A monitoring system can therefore infer a structural property of the workload from the empirical distribution of its overshoot.

**What did not survive.** Two attractive conjectures are false and worth recording. (i) *Randomisation improves the worst case.* False: Theorem 6.2 holds at every phase, so no phase distribution lowers the supremum. (ii) *The dyadic grid is optimal.* False as stated: $e$ is the unique optimum and $3$ is closer to it than $2$; the honest version is Theorem 7.4. A third statement, the strict AM–GM gap $\sqrt\rho < (\rho-1)/\log\rho$, was first conjectured from numerics and then proved (Theorem 6.8) via the perfect-square derivative identity.

**Limitations.** The model treats each class's allocation independently, with no global capacity constraint coupling them; a constrained version (allocate $\sum_y \mathrm{service}(y) \le 1$) would make the arbiter's rounding decisions interdependent, and the sharp constants there are open. The jitter analysis averages over a *uniform* phase; one may ask whether a non-uniform phase distribution optimises some other functional of the slack (it cannot change the sup or inf, by Corollary 6.3, but it can change every moment in between). Finally, the geometric demand ladder of Section 8 is the simplest non-trivial dynamics; general demand processes require an ergodic-theoretic rather than a Diophantine treatment.

---

## 11. Future work

**Sub-$\rho$ slack for state-dependent arbiters.** The factor $\rho$ is forced only because the arbiter is *memoryless*: each request is rounded independently, so the log-slack is a fixed point of the shift on $\mathbb{R}/\log\rho\,\mathbb{Z}$. An arbiter carrying a deficit counter between rounds can *borrow* from a round whose slack is small. The natural conjecture is that the long-run *average* slack of the optimal state-dependent arbiter equals the geometric mean $\sqrt\rho$, not $\rho$, while the *per-round* worst case remains $\rho$. Cycle-averaged results of Section 6 give the target constant; what is needed is a matching lower bound over all causal deficit policies.

**Quantitative equidistribution.** Theorem 8.7 is qualitative. For a badly-approximable growth ratio (bounded continued-fraction partial quotients, e.g. $\log_2\alpha$ with quadratic-irrational-like behaviour), the discrepancy of the slack orbit after $N$ rounds should be $O(\log N/N)$, giving an explicit bound on how many rounds an operator must wait before observing a slack within $\varepsilon$ of the ceiling. Conversely, Liouville-type ratios would give arbitrarily long stretches of nearly constant slack.

**Multi-class coupling.** With a hard channel constraint the arbiter must round some classes down; the resulting object is a simultaneous Diophantine approximation problem, and the sharp constant should depend on the number of classes.

**Non-uniform phase distributions.** Characterise which functionals of the slack distribution are optimised by which phase laws, given that the sup and inf are immovable.

---

## 12. Conclusion

Quantisation in a thermodynamically fair scheduler costs exactly the grid ratio, and nothing can be shaved from either end: the achievable slack set is exactly $[1,\rho)$, closed at $1$ and open at $\rho$, with the openness explained structurally by log-periodicity. Randomising the grid leaves the guarantee untouched but sets the typical cost at $\sqrt\rho$ and the mean cost at $(\rho-1)/\log\rho$, strictly ordered below $\rho$. The best grid ratio is Euler's number; the ubiquitous choice $\rho = 2$ costs under $7\%$ more and ties exactly with $\rho = 4$. And whether a given running exchange ever feels the worst case is settled by a single arithmetic question about its growth ratio: dense slack if and only if $\log_2\alpha$ is irrational. Tripling demand each round eventually meets every inefficiency the design permits; quadrupling it never wastes a slot.

\begin{abstract}
We analyse the exact cost of quantisation in a thermodynamically-motivated fair-scheduling model. \section{Introduction}

\subsection{The physical setting}

Consider a shared quantum channel --- an optical fibre, a satellite downlink, a bus of entanglement-distribution nodes --- multiplexed across several \emph{transport classes}. Each class $y$ carries an \emph{occupancy} $p(y)\in(0,1]$ (the probability that a slot offered to $y$ is usable), a \emph{demand} $d(y)>0$, and a \emph{reservation credit} $r(y)\in\mathbb{R}$. Three global constants govern the exchange: an inverse temperature $\beta>0$, a scheduling quantum $\gamma>0$, and a background cost $M\in\mathbb{R}$.

\begin{definition}[Photon-transport exchange]
A \emph{photon-transport exchange} over an index set $\iota$ consists of constants $\beta>0$, $\gamma>0$, $M\in\mathbb{R}$ and functions $p,d,r:\iota\to\mathbb{R}$ with $0<p(y)\le 1$, $d(y)>0$, and
\[
\beta\log\!\big(1/p(y)\big) + M + \gamma - r(y) > 0 \qquad\text{for all } y .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Transport gap and ideal share]
The \emph{transport gap} of class $y$ is
\[
\gapop(y) = \beta\log\!\big(1/p(y)\big) + M + \gamma - r(y) > 0,
\]
the Boltzmann cost of one successful transfer corrected by the class's credit, and the \emph{ideal share} is
\[
\idealop(y) = \frac{\gamma\, d(y)}{\gapop(y)} > 0 .
\]
\end{definition}

A rare class ($p(y)$ small, hence $\log(1/p(y))$ large) has a large gap and a small ideal share; a class with a large credit has a small gap and a large share. Monotonicity is immediate: comparing two classes of the same exchange with $M - r(y) = M - r(z)$, we have $p(y)\le p(z) \Rightarrow \gapop(z)\le\gapop(y)$.

\subsection{The quantisation constraint}

\begin{definition}[Grid quantiser]
For a grid ratio $\rho>1$ and $x>0$, set $\gridceil_\rho(x) = \rho^{\lceil \log_\rho x\rceil}$, the least integer power of $\rho$ (positive or negative exponent) that is at least $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Delivered service and slack]
The grid-$\rho$ arbiter delivers $\serviceop_\rho(y) = \gridceil_\rho(\idealop(y))$; the \emph{dyadic} arbiter is $\rho=2$, written $\serviceop(y) = 2^{\lceil\log_2\idealop(y)\rceil}$. The \emph{slack} is $\serviceop(y)/\idealop(y)$; for a request size $x>0$ we write $\slackop(x) = \gridceil_2(x)/x$ and $\logslackop(x) = \log_2\slackop(x)$.
\end{definition}

The organising question: \emph{exactly what does quantisation cost?}

\section{The grid quantiser}

Fix $\rho>1$ and let $x>0$.

\begin{lemma}[Covering]\label{lem:cover}
$x \le \gridceil_\rho(x)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $x = \rho^{\log_\rho x}$. Since $\log_\rho x \le \lceil\log_\rho x\rceil$ and $t\mapsto\rho^t$ is increasing, $x\le\rho^{\lceil\log_\rho x\rceil}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Efficiency]\label{lem:eff}
$\gridceil_\rho(x) < \rho x$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$\lceil t\rceil < t+1$, so $\rho^{\lceil\log_\rho x\rceil} < \rho^{\log_\rho x + 1} = \rho x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Forced jump]\label{lem:jump}
If $1 < x \le \rho$ then $\gridceil_\rho(x) = \rho$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$0 < \log_\rho x \le 1$, so $\lceil\log_\rho x\rceil = 1$.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:jump} is the workhorse for every sharpness construction: on the whole interval $(1,\rho]$ the quantiser delivers the same window $\rho$, so the slack $\rho/x$ sweeps $[1,\rho)$.

\begin{lemma}[Exactness on the grid]\label{lem:exact}
$\gridceil_\rho(x) = x$ if and only if $x = \rho^k$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Take $k=\lceil\log_\rho x\rceil$. ($\Leftarrow$) $\log_\rho\rho^k = k\in\mathbb{Z}$, so the ceiling is $k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Equivariance and log-periodicity]\label{lem:equi}
$\gridceil_\rho(\rho x) = \rho\,\gridceil_\rho(x)$, hence
$\gridceil_\rho(\rho x)/(\rho x) = \gridceil_\rho(x)/x$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$\log_\rho(\rho x) = \log_\rho x + 1$ and $\lceil t+1\rceil = \lceil t\rceil + 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity]
$0 < x \le y$ implies $\gridceil_\rho(x)\le\gridceil_\rho(y)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$\log_\rho$, $\lceil\cdot\rceil$ and $t\mapsto\rho^t$ are all monotone.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:equi} already explains the shape of the answer: on the logarithmic scale the slack is periodic with period $\log\rho$, and on one period it is $x\mapsto\rho/x$ on $(1,\rho]$, of range $[1,\rho)$ --- closed below, open above.

\section{The floor, the ceiling, and the dyadic spectrum}

\begin{theorem}[No starvation]\label{thm:floor}
For every exchange and every class,
\[
\frac{\gamma\,d(y)}{\beta\log(1/p(y)) + M + \gamma - r(y)} \;\le\; \serviceop(y).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The left side is $\idealop(y)>0$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:cover} with $\rho=2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Factor-two ceiling]\label{thm:ceil}
$\serviceop(y) < 2\,\idealop(y)$ for every exchange and every class.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:eff} with $\rho=2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:ico}
$\serviceop(y)/\idealop(y)\in[1,2)$ always.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Exactness criterion]\label{thm:exactcrit}
$\serviceop(y) = \idealop(y)$ if and only if $\idealop(y) = 2^k$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:exact}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Witness exchange]\label{def:witness}
For $x>0$ let $W_x$ be the single-class exchange with $\beta=\gamma=M=1$, $p\equiv 1$, $r\equiv 1$, $d\equiv x$.
\end{definition}

Since $\log(1/1)=0$, the gap of $W_x$ is $0+1+1-1=1$ and $\idealop_{W_x} = x$: the witness family realises any prescribed ideal share, so all questions about the slack spectrum reduce to questions about $\gridceil$.

\begin{theorem}[The slack spectrum is exactly $[1,2)$]\label{thm:spectrum}
\[
\big\{ c\in\mathbb{R} : \exists\ \text{an exchange and a class with } \serviceop(y) = c\,\idealop(y)\big\} = [1,2).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\subseteq$) Corollary~\ref{cor:ico}. ($\supseteq$) Given $t\in[1,2)$ put $x = 2/t$; then $x>1$ since $t<2$ and $x\le 2$ since $t\ge 1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:jump}, $\serviceop_{W_x} = 2 = t\cdot(2/t) = t\,\idealop_{W_x}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The floor is attained and optimal]
$W_1$ has $\idealop = 1 = 2^0$, so its service equals its ideal share exactly by Theorem~\ref{thm:exactcrit}. Hence no constant $c>1$ satisfies $c\,\idealop(y)\le\serviceop(y)$ for all exchanges.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[The ceiling is optimal]\label{cor:ceilopt}
For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an exchange with $(2-\varepsilon)\idealop(y) < \serviceop(y)$; hence no $c<2$ satisfies $\serviceop(y)\le c\,\idealop(y)$ for all exchanges.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $x = 1 + \min(\varepsilon/4,1/2)$, so $1<x\le 2$ and $\serviceop_{W_x} = 2$. If $\varepsilon\ge 2$ then $(2-\varepsilon)x < 2$ trivially; if $\varepsilon<2$ it is equivalent to $x-1 < \varepsilon/(2-\varepsilon)$, which holds since $x-1\le\varepsilon/4$ and $2-\varepsilon<4$.
\end{proof}

Thus the guiding claim --- \emph{the no-starvation constant cannot be improved beyond a factor of $2$} --- holds in the strongest possible form: $\serviceop < 2\,\idealop$ universally, the value $1$ is attained, and $2$ is the exact supremum.

\section{Where the factor two comes from}

\begin{theorem}[General grid witness]\label{thm:gridwitness}
For every $\rho>1$ and $t\in[1,\rho)$ the exchange $W_{\rho/t}$ satisfies $\serviceop_\rho(y) = t\,\idealop(y)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
With $x = \rho/t$ we have $1<x\le\rho$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:jump} gives $\serviceop_\rho = \rho = t\cdot(\rho/t)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal ceiling constant]\label{thm:optceil}
For $\rho>1$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\big(\forall\ \text{exchanges}: \serviceop_\rho(y)\le c\,\idealop(y)\big) \iff \rho \le c .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) Lemma~\ref{lem:eff}. ($\Rightarrow$) If $c<\rho$, put $t = \max(1,(c+\rho)/2)$; then $1\le t<\rho$ and $t>c$. Theorem~\ref{thm:gridwitness} gives an exchange of slack exactly $t>c$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal floor constant]\label{thm:optfloor}
For $\rho>1$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\big(\forall\ \text{exchanges}: c\,\idealop(y)\le \serviceop_\rho(y)\big) \iff c \le 1 .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) Lemma~\ref{lem:cover}. ($\Rightarrow$) Theorem~\ref{thm:gridwitness} with $t=1$ gives an exchange with $\serviceop_\rho=\idealop$, forcing $c\le 1$.
\end{proof}

Specialising to $\rho = 2$: the factor $2$ in the headline statement is precisely the grid ratio of the arbiter --- nothing else.

\section{Aggregation and non-vacuity}

\begin{theorem}[The floor aggregates]
For a finite family of classes, $\sum_y \idealop(y) \le \sum_y \serviceop(y)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Sum Theorem~\ref{thm:floor} termwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The ceiling aggregates]
For a finite nonempty family, $\sum_y \serviceop(y) < 2\sum_y \idealop(y)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Sum the strict inequality of Theorem~\ref{thm:ceil} over a nonempty index set.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rare channels are squeezed out]
For any $\varepsilon>0$, if $\gapop(y) > 2\gamma d(y)/\varepsilon$ then $\serviceop(y)<\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The hypothesis rearranges to $2\,\idealop(y)<\varepsilon$; combine with Theorem~\ref{thm:ceil}.
\end{proof}

As $p(y)\to 0$ the Boltzmann cost diverges and service tends to $0$: the floor of Theorem~\ref{thm:floor} is a genuine, saturating constraint, not a bookkeeping tautology.

\section{Phase-jittered arbiters}

\begin{definition}[Jittered quantiser]
For $\rho>1$, phase $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$, $x>0$, set
$J_{\rho,\theta}(x) = \rho^{\lceil \log_\rho x - \theta\rceil + \theta}$: the ladder $\rho^{\mathbb{Z}}$ shifted multiplicatively by $\rho^\theta$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The guarantee is phase-independent]\label{thm:jitterbound}
For every $\rho>1$, every $\theta$ and every $x>0$, $x \le J_{\rho,\theta}(x) < \rho x$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
With $t = \log_\rho x - \theta$, $\lceil t\rceil\ge t$ gives $\lceil t\rceil+\theta\ge\log_\rho x$, and $\lceil t\rceil<t+1$ gives $\lceil t\rceil+\theta<\log_\rho x + 1$; apply monotonicity of $\rho^{(\cdot)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Randomisation cannot help the worst case]\label{cor:norand}
The two-sided bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:jitterbound} is attained in the limit at every fixed phase, so no probability distribution over phases lowers the supremum of the slack below $\rho$ nor raises its infimum above $1$. The conjecture ``randomisation improves the worst case'' is false for this family.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[The log-slack is a circle rotation]\label{thm:rot}
For $\rho>1$, $x>0$ and every $\theta$,
\[
\log_\rho\!\left(\frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\right) = \fracpart{\theta - \log_\rho x},
\]
where $\fracpart{t} = t - \lfloor t\rfloor$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The left side equals $\lceil u\rceil - u$ with $u = \log_\rho x - \theta$, and $\lceil u\rceil - u = \fracpart{-u}$ (checked separately for $u\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $u\notin\mathbb{Z}$).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Mean log-slack]\label{thm:meanlog}
For every $\rho>1$, $x>0$,
\[
\int_0^1 \log_\rho\!\left(\frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\right) d\theta = \frac12,
\qquad
\int_0^1 \log\!\left(\frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\right) d\theta = \frac{\log\rho}{2}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Substitute Theorem~\ref{thm:rot} and translate: the integrand is a $1$-periodic function of $\theta$, and $\int_0^1\fracpart{t}\,dt = 1/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Geometric-mean slack]\label{thm:geo}
For every $\rho>1$ and $x>0$,
$\exp\!\left(\int_0^1 \log(J_{\rho,\theta}(x)/x)\,d\theta\right) = \sqrt\rho$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:meanlog}.
\end{proof}

The typical slack does not depend on $x$, hence not on the exchange; for $\rho=2$ it is $\sqrt2\approx 1.4142$.

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic-mean slack]\label{thm:arith}
For every $\rho>1$ and $x>0$,
$\displaystyle \int_0^1 \frac{J_{\rho,\theta}(x)}{x}\,d\theta = \frac{\rho-1}{\log\rho}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:rot} the integrand is $\rho^{\fracpart{\theta-\log_\rho x}}$, a $1$-periodic function of $\theta$; translating reduces the integral to $\int_0^1 \rho^s\,ds = \int_0^1 e^{s\log\rho}\,ds = (\rho-1)/\log\rho$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict hierarchy of the three constants]\label{thm:hier}
For every $\rho>1$,
\[
\sqrt\rho \;<\; \frac{\rho-1}{\log\rho} \;<\; \rho .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Left.} Put $u=\sqrt\rho>1$; the claim becomes $2\log u < u - 1/u$. Let $f(u) = u - 1/u - 2\log u$. Then $f(1)=0$ and
\[
f'(u) = 1 + \frac{1}{u^2} - \frac{2}{u} = \Big(1-\frac1u\Big)^2 > 0 \quad (u>1),
\]
a perfect square, so $f$ is strictly increasing on $[1,\infty)$ and $f(u)>0$ for $u>1$.
\emph{Right.} From $\log t < t-1$ for $t>0$, $t\ne 1$, with $t = 1/\rho$: $-\log\rho < 1/\rho - 1$, i.e. $\log\rho > (\rho-1)/\rho$; multiply by $\rho/\log\rho>0$.
\end{proof}

For the dyadic arbiter: $1.4142\ldots < 1.4427\ldots < 2$. Jitter leaves the guarantee untouched but converts the worst-case factor into a typical factor $\sqrt\rho$ and a mean factor $(\rho-1)/\log\rho$.

\section{The optimal grid ratio}

\begin{definition}[Grid cost]
$C(\rho) = \dfrac{\rho}{\log\rho}$ for $\rho>1$: worst-case slack per unit of logarithmic dynamic range covered by one backoff level.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Euler's number is the unique optimum]\label{thm:e}
For every $\rho>1$, $e \le C(\rho)$, with equality if and only if $\rho = e$; and $C(e) = e$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply $\log t \le t-1$ with $t = \rho/e$: $\log\rho - 1 \le \rho/e - 1$, so $e\log\rho\le\rho$, i.e. $e\le C(\rho)$. Strictness holds unless $t = 1$, i.e. unless $\rho = e$; and $C(e) = e/1 = e$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Binary and quaternary arbiters tie exactly]
$C(4) = C(2)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\log 4 = 2\log 2$, so $C(4) = 4/(2\log 2) = 2/\log 2 = C(2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The dyadic arbiter is within $7\%$ of optimal]
$C(2) < 1.07\,e$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$C(2) = 2/\log 2$. With $\log 2 > 0.6931471803$ and $e>2.7182818283$ one gets $2/\log 2 < 2.8854 < 1.07\,e$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Against over-claiming]
``The dyadic grid is optimal'' is \emph{false}: $e$ is the unique optimum, and $3$ is closer to it than $2$ is, with $C(3) = 3/\log 3 \approx 2.7307$ against $C(2)\approx 2.8854$ and $e\approx 2.7183$. The defensible statements are the quantitative $7\%$ bound and the exact tie $C(2)=C(4)$, which explains why doubling the window is a natural fixed point of the design trade-off.
\end{remark}

\section{Diophantine dynamics: sharpness inside a single exchange}

Sections~3--4 quantify over the space of exchanges. We now fix one exchange whose demand grows geometrically by a factor $\alpha>0$ per round, so the ideal share runs along the ladder $\alpha^n$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. By Definition~\ref{def:witness} every such ladder is realised by a genuine exchange, and its $\serviceop/\idealop$ is exactly $\slackop(\alpha^n)$.

\begin{lemma}[Log-slack is a ceiling defect]\label{lem:defect}
For $x>0$, $\logslackop(x) = \fracpart{-\log_2 x}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$\slackop(x) = 2^{\lceil\log_2 x\rceil - \log_2 x}$, and $\lceil u\rceil - u = \fracpart{-u}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The demand ladder is a circle rotation]\label{thm:ladder}
For $\alpha>0$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\logslackop(\alpha^n) = \fracpart{n\cdot(-\log_2\alpha)}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\log_2(\alpha^n) = n\log_2\alpha$; substitute into Lemma~\ref{lem:defect}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Kronecker's theorem, in the form needed]\label{thm:kron}
Let $\vartheta$ be irrational. For every $y\in(0,1)$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $|\fracpart{n\vartheta} - y| < \varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The additive subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$ generated by $\vartheta$ and $1$ is dense exactly when $\vartheta\notin\mathbb{Q}$ (a closed subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$ is cyclic or all of $\mathbb{R}$; cyclicity would force $\vartheta$ rational). Put $\delta = \min(\varepsilon, y, 1-y)>0$ and choose a group element $z = m\vartheta + k$ with $|z-y|<\delta$. Then $0<z<1$, so $\fracpart{m\vartheta} = \fracpart{z-k} = z$, and $|\fracpart{m\vartheta}-y|<\delta\le\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dense slack orbit in the irrational case]\label{thm:dense}
If $\alpha>0$ and $\log_2\alpha$ is irrational then for every $s\in(0,1)$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $|\logslackop(\alpha^n) - s| < \varepsilon$, and consequently
\[
[0,1] \subseteq \overline{\{\logslackop(\alpha^n) : n\in\mathbb{Z}\}} .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:kron} with $\vartheta = -\log_2\alpha$ and use Theorem~\ref{thm:ladder}; the orbit closure contains $(0,1)$, and taking closures again with $\overline{(0,1)}=[0,1]$ and idempotence of closure gives the display.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A single exchange saturates both ends]\label{thm:sat}
If $\log_2\alpha$ is irrational and $0<\varepsilon<1$ then
\[
\exists\,n\in\mathbb{Z}:\ \slackop(\alpha^n) > 2^{\,1-\varepsilon},
\qquad
\exists\,m\in\mathbb{Z}:\ \slackop(\alpha^m) < 2^{\,\varepsilon}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:dense} with target $s = 1-\varepsilon/2$ and tolerance $\varepsilon/4$, so $\logslackop(\alpha^n) > 1 - \tfrac34\varepsilon > 1-\varepsilon$; since $\slackop = 2^{\logslackop}$ and $t\mapsto 2^t$ is increasing, the first claim follows. Symmetrically with $s=\varepsilon/2$ for the second.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Periodicity and finiteness in the rational case]\label{thm:per}
If $\log_2\alpha = p/q$ with $q\ne 0$ integers, then $\logslackop(\alpha^{n+kq}) = \logslackop(\alpha^n)$ for all $n,k\in\mathbb{Z}$. If moreover $q>0$, the orbit $\{\logslackop(\alpha^n) : n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ has at most $q$ elements, is closed, and is not dense in $[0,1]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:ladder}, $\logslackop(\alpha^{n+kq}) = \fracpart{n(-p/q) - kp} = \fracpart{n(-p/q)}$. Every $n$ is congruent mod $q$ to an element of $\{0,\dots,q-1\}$, so the orbit is the image of a finite set; a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed and cannot contain the infinite set $[0,1]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Diophantine dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
For $\alpha>0$,
\[
[0,1] \subseteq \overline{\{\logslackop(\alpha^n) : n\in\mathbb{Z}\}}
\iff
\log_2\alpha \ \text{is irrational}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) Theorem~\ref{thm:dense}. ($\Rightarrow$) If $\log_2\alpha$ is rational, write it as $p/q$ with $q>0$; Theorem~\ref{thm:per} shows the orbit is finite, hence not dense.
\end{proof}

Sharpness for a fixed exchange is therefore a Diophantine property of the growth ratio, not a scheduling property.

\begin{theorem}[$\log_2 3$ is irrational]\label{thm:log23}
$\log_2 3\notin\mathbb{Q}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $\log_2 3>0$, a rational representation may be taken as $p/q$ with $p,q$ positive integers. Then $q\log 3 = p\log 2$, so $3^q = 2^p$: the left side is odd and exceeds $1$, the right side is even. Contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Ternary growth saturates the spectrum]
If demand grows by a factor $3$ per round then $[0,1]\subseteq\overline{\{\logslackop(3^n)\}}$; quantitatively, for every $0<\varepsilon<1$ some round has slack exceeding $2^{1-\varepsilon}$ and some round has slack below $2^\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorems~\ref{thm:dense}, \ref{thm:sat}, \ref{thm:log23}.
\end{proof}

By contrast $\alpha = 4$ has $\log_2 4 = 2\in\mathbb{Z}$, so every $\alpha^n$ lies on the dyadic grid and the slack is identically $1$; and $\alpha = \sqrt2$ has $\log_2\alpha = 1/2$, giving a period-$2$ orbit with slack values $\{1,\sqrt2\}$.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Dyadic allocation]
Given $\beta,\gamma,M$ and per-class $(p,d,r)$: compute $\gapop = \beta\log(1/p)+M+\gamma-r$; abort if $\gapop\le 0$; compute $\idealop = \gamma d/\gapop$; return $2^{\lceil\log_2\idealop\rceil}$. Cost $O(1)$ per class. Numerically, the ceiling must snap to an integer when $\log_2\idealop$ is within floating-point epsilon of one; otherwise a share that is exactly a power of two may be rounded to the next window and the reported slack jumps spuriously from $1$ to $2$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Slack-orbit sampler]
Given $\alpha$ and a horizon $N$, return $(\fracpart{-n\log_2\alpha})_{n=0}^{N-1}$ together with the star discrepancy of the sample. Cost $O(N\log N)$ with sorting. For irrational $\log_2\alpha$ the discrepancy tends to $0$; for $\log_2\alpha = p/q$ in lowest terms it stalls near $1/(2q)$, giving a numerical test of Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy}.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Grid-cost optimiser]
Minimise $C(\rho) = \rho/\log\rho$ over $\rho>1$. Since $C'(\rho) = (\log\rho-1)/(\log\rho)^2$, the unique stationary point is $\rho=e$, with $C$ strictly decreasing on $(1,e)$ and strictly increasing on $(e,\infty)$; bisection on $C'$ or golden-section search converges in $O(\log(1/\mathrm{tol}))$ evaluations. In practice the routine reports the relative excess $C(\rho)/e - 1$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Applications and discussion}

\paragraph{Admission control.} Theorem~\ref{thm:floor} is the safety property a scheduler advertises. Theorem~\ref{thm:optceil} says the corresponding capacity reservation must be $\rho$ times the sum of ideal shares and that this factor cannot be shaved: any admission controller provisioning less can be defeated by an adversarial demand vector.

\paragraph{Capacity planning.} For expected throughput the binding constant is $(\rho-1)/\log\rho$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:arith}), or $\sqrt\rho$ when slacks combine multiplicatively across independent stages (Theorem~\ref{thm:geo}). For $\rho=2$ that is a planning factor of $1.44$ rather than $2$ --- a $28\%$ difference in provisioned capacity, entirely accounted for by which mean is appropriate.

\paragraph{Grid design.} A designer free to choose the ratio should choose $e$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:e}); $\rho=2$ costs at most $7\%$ more, and $\rho=4$ costs exactly the same as $\rho=2$. Restricted to integer ratios, $\rho=3$ is within half a percent of optimal.

\paragraph{Diagnostics.} If a running class exhibits a constant slack, or cycles through a short finite list, its demand growth ratio is a rational power of the grid ratio. If the observed slack wanders densely over $[1,2)$, the growth ratio is Diophantine-generic. A monitoring system can thus infer a structural property of the workload from the empirical distribution of its overshoot.

\paragraph{What did not survive.} Two attractive conjectures are false. (i) \emph{Randomisation improves the worst case}: false by Corollary~\ref{cor:norand}. (ii) \emph{The dyadic grid is optimal}: false as stated; $e$ is optimal and $3$ is closer to it than $2$. The strict AM--GM gap $\sqrt\rho<(\rho-1)/\log\rho$ was first conjectured from numerics and then proved (Theorem~\ref{thm:hier}) via the perfect-square derivative identity.

\paragraph{Limitations.} The model allocates to each class independently, with no global capacity constraint coupling them; a constrained version makes the rounding decisions interdependent and the sharp constants there are open. The jitter analysis averages over a uniform phase. The geometric demand ladder is the simplest non-trivial dynamics; general demand processes need an ergodic rather than a Diophantine treatment.

\section{Future work}

\paragraph{Sub-$\rho$ slack for state-dependent arbiters.} The factor $\rho$ is forced only because the arbiter is memoryless: each request is rounded independently, so the log-slack is a fixed point of the shift on $\mathbb{R}/\log\rho\,\mathbb{Z}$. An arbiter carrying a deficit counter between rounds can borrow from a round whose slack is small, and the natural conjecture is that the long-run average slack of the optimal state-dependent arbiter equals the geometric mean $\sqrt\rho$, not $\rho$, while the per-round worst case remains $\rho$. What is needed is a matching lower bound over all causal deficit policies.

\paragraph{Quantitative equidistribution.} Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy} is qualitative. For a badly-approximable growth ratio the discrepancy of the slack orbit after $N$ rounds should be $O(\log N/N)$, giving an explicit bound on how many rounds an operator must wait before observing a slack within $\varepsilon$ of the ceiling; Liouville-type ratios would give arbitrarily long stretches of nearly constant slack.

\paragraph{Multi-class coupling.} With a hard channel constraint the arbiter must round some classes down; the resulting object is a simultaneous Diophantine approximation problem, and the sharp constant should depend on the number of classes.

\section{Conclusion}

Quantisation in a thermodynamically fair scheduler costs exactly the grid ratio, and nothing can be shaved from either end: the achievable slack set is exactly $[1,\rho)$, closed at $1$ and open at $\rho$, with the openness explained structurally by log-periodicity. Randomising the grid leaves the guarantee untouched but sets the typical cost at $\sqrt\rho$ and the mean cost at $(\rho-1)/\log\rho$, strictly ordered below $\rho$. The best grid ratio is Euler's number; the ubiquitous $\rho=2$ costs under $7\%$ more and ties exactly with $\rho=4$. Whether a given running exchange ever feels the worst case is settled by one arithmetic question about its growth ratio: dense slack if and only if $\log_2\alpha$ is irrational.

EPS: float = 1e-12


def grid_ceil(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Smallest integer power of `rho` that is >= `x`.

    The naive `rho ** ceil(log(x, rho))` misfires when `x` is exactly a power of
    `rho`: floating point may return `log` a hair above the integer, and the
    quantiser then jumps a whole level, reporting a slack of `rho` instead of 1.
    We snap the logarithm to an integer when it is within EPS of one.
    """
    if rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("grid ratio must exceed 1")
    if x <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("request size must be positive")
    t: float = math.log(x) / math.log(rho)
    nearest: int = round(t)
    k: int = nearest if abs(t - nearest) < EPS else math.ceil(t)
    return float(rho) ** k


def slack(rho: float, x: float) -> float:

def demo_jitter() -> None:
    rule("4. Jitter: worst case unchanged, typical case sqrt(rho), mean (rho-1)/log rho")

    def jitter_ceil(rho: float, theta: float, x: float) -> float:
        t = math.log(x) / math.log(rho) - theta
        nearest = round(t)
        k = nearest if abs(t - nearest) < EPS else math.ceil(t)
        return rho ** (k + theta)

    n_phase = 200000
    for rho in (2.0, math.e, 3.0, 4.0):
        x = 1.3719  # an arbitrary, generic request size
        worst = 0.0
        geo_log_sum = 0.0
        arith_sum = 0.0
        for j in range(n_phase):
            theta = (j + 0.5) / n_phase
            s = jitter_ceil(rho, theta, x) / x
            assert 1.0 <= s < rho + 1e-12, "phase-independent bound violated"
            worst = max(worst, s)
            geo_log_sum += math.log(s)
            arith_sum += s
        geo = math.exp(geo_log_sum / n_phase)
        ari = arith_sum / n_phase
        print(f"  rho = {rho:6.4f}:  sup over phases = {worst:.6f} (theory {rho:.6f});"
              f"  geometric mean = {geo:.6f} (theory {math.sqrt(rho):.6f});")
        print(f"{'':16}arithmetic mean = {ari:.6f} "
              f"(theory {(rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho):.6f})")
        assert abs(geo - math.sqrt(rho)) < 1e-4
        assert abs(ari - (rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho)) < 1e-4
        assert math.sqrt(rho) < (rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho) < rho

    print("\nRandomisation never lowers the supremum: the bound 1 <= slack < rho")
    print("holds at every single phase, so no phase law can beat it.")


def demo_grid_cost() -> None:
    rule("5. The grid cost rho/log(rho) is uniquely minimised at rho = e")

    def grid_cost(rho: float) -> float:
        return rho / math.log(rho)

    print(f"{'rho':>8} {'C(rho)':>12} {'excess over e':>16}")
    for rho in (1.5, 2.0, 2.5, math.e, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 8.0, 16.0):
        c = grid_cost(rho)
        print(f"{rho:8.4f} {c:12.6f} {100.0 * (c / math.e - 1.0):15.3f}%")
        assert c >= math.e - 1e-12

    print(f"\n  C(2) = {grid_cost(2.0):.9f}")
    print(f"  C(4) = {grid_cost(4.0):.9f}   (exactly equal to C(2))")
    print(f"  C(3) = {grid_cost(3.0):.9f}   (closest integer ratio to the optimum)")
    print(f"  e    = {math.e:.9f}")
    assert abs(grid_cost(4.0) - grid_cost(2.0)) < 1e-12
    assert grid_cost(2.0) < 1.07 * math.e

    # golden-section search recovers the optimum
    lo, hi = 1.2, 10.0
    inv_phi = (math.sqrt(5.0) - 1.0) / 2.0
    for _ in range(200):
        a = hi - inv_phi * (hi - lo)
        b = lo + inv_phi * (hi - lo)
        if grid_cost(a) < grid_cost(b):
            hi = b
        else:
            lo = a
    print(f"  golden-section minimiser: rho* = {(lo + hi) / 2:.12f}  (e = {math.e:.12f})")
    assert abs((lo + hi) / 2 - math.e) < 1e-6


def star_discrepancy(sample: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Exact star discrepancy of a finite sample of [0,1)."""
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    d = 0.0
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        d = max(d, abs((i + 1) / n - x), abs(i / n - x))
    return d


def demo_dichotomy() -> None:
    rule("6. Diophantine dichotomy: dense slack orbit iff log2(alpha) is irrational")
    print("Demand grows by a factor alpha per round; the ideal share climbs alpha^n")
    print("and the log-slack is frac(-n log2 alpha), an orbit of a circle rotation.\n")

    # Rational exponents are handled with exact fractions, so that the finite
    # orbit is reported exactly rather than being smeared by floating-point drift.
    rational_cases: List[Tuple[str, Fraction]] = [
        ("alpha = 4      (log2 alpha = 2)",     Fraction(2, 1)),
        ("alpha = sqrt2  (log2 alpha = 1/2)",   Fraction(1, 2)),
        ("alpha = 2**(3/7)",                    Fraction(3, 7)),
    ]
    irrational_cases: List[Tuple[str, float]] = [
        ("alpha = 3      (log2 3 irrational)",  3.0),
        ("alpha = 10     (log2 10 irrational)", 10.0),
        ("alpha = pi",                          math.pi),
    ]
    N = 4000
    header = (f"{'case':>36} {'#distinct':>10} {'discrepancy':>13} "
              f"{'min slack':>10} {'max slack':>10}")
    print(header)
    for label, theta in rational_cases:
        orbit_q = [(-n * theta) % 1 for n in range(N)]
        distinct = len(set(orbit_q))
        orbit = [float(v) for v in orbit_q]
        slacks = [2.0 ** v for v in orbit]
        print(f"{label:>36} {distinct:10d} {star_discrepancy(orbit):13.6f} "
              f"{min(slacks):10.6f} {max(slacks):10.6f}")
        assert distinct == theta.denominator, "orbit period must be the denominator"
    for label, alpha in irrational_cases:
        orbit = [frac(-n * math.log2(alpha)) for n in range(N)]
        distinct = len({round(v, 9) for v in orbit})
        disc = star_discrepancy(orbit)
        slacks = [2.0 ** v for v in orbit]
        print(f"{label:>36} {distinct:10d} {disc:13.6f} "
              f"{min(slacks):10.6f} {max(slacks):10.6f}")
        assert disc < 0.01, "irrational case must equidistribute"

    print("\nQuantitative saturation for ternary growth (alpha = 3), searching n >= 1:")
    theta3 = math.log2(3.0)
    horizon = 200000
    hi_n = max(range(1, horizon), key=lambda n: frac(-n * theta3))
    lo_n = min(range(1, horizon), key=lambda n: frac(-n * theta3))
    hi_s = 2.0 ** frac(-hi_n * theta3)
    lo_s = 2.0 ** frac(-lo_n * theta3)
    print(f"  best overshoot : n = {hi_n:6d}, slack = {hi_s:.9f}  (ceiling 2)")
    print(f"  best efficiency: m = {lo_n:6d}, slack = {lo_s:.9f}  (floor 1)")
    for eps in (0.5, 0.2, 0.05, 0.01):
        print(f"  eps = {eps:5.2f}:  {hi_s:.9f} > 2^(1-eps) = {2.0 ** (1 - eps):.6f}   and   "
              f"{lo_s:.9f} < 2^eps = {2.0 ** eps:.6f}")
        assert hi_s > 2.0 ** (1 - eps) and lo_s < 2.0 ** eps

    print("\nBy contrast, alpha = 4 has slack identically 1: perfect efficiency forever.")
    assert all(abs(slack(2.0, 4.0 ** n) - 1.0) < 1e-12 for n in range(-20, 21))

def grid_ceil(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Smallest integer power of `rho` that is >= `x`.

    The naive `rho ** ceil(log(x, rho))` misfires when `x` is exactly a power of
    `rho`: floating point may return `log` a hair above the integer, and the
    quantiser then jumps a whole level, reporting a slack of `rho` instead of 1.
    We snap the logarithm to an integer when it is within EPS of one.
    """
    if rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("grid ratio must exceed 1")
    if x <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("request size must be positive")
    t: float = math.log(x) / math.log(rho)
    nearest: int = round(t)
    k: int = nearest if abs(t - nearest) < EPS else math.ceil(t)
    return float(rho) ** k


def slack(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Multiplicative overshoot gridCeil_rho(x) / x, always in [1, rho)."""
    return grid_ceil(rho, x) / x


def log_slack(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Overshoot measured in backoff levels; equals frac(-log_rho x)."""
    return math.log(slack(rho, x)) / math.log(rho)

    goal = math.log2(threshold)

    return None

@dataclass(frozen=True)

    name: str

    d: float
    r: float

    name: str

def grid_ceil(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Least integer power of `rho` that is at least `x`.

    The logarithm is snapped to the nearest integer when it is within `_LOG_SNAP`
    of one; without this guard a share that sits exactly on the grid can be pushed
    to the next rung by floating-point error, inflating the reported overshoot
    from 1 all the way to rho.

    if rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("grid ratio must exceed 1")
    if x <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("request size must be positive")
    t: float = math.log(x) / math.log(rho)
    nearest: int = round(t)
    k: int = nearest if abs(t - nearest) < _LOG_SNAP else math.ceil(t)
    return float(rho) ** k

    gamma: float,
    M: float,
    classes: Sequence[TransportClass],
    rho: float = 2.0,

    Raises ValueError if a class has a non-positive transport gap, which is the
    admissibility condition of the model.

    if beta <= 0.0 or gamma <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("beta and gamma must be positive")
    out: List[Allocation] = []
    for c in classes:

            raise ValueError(f"{c.name}: occupancy must lie in (0,1]")
        if c.d <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError(f"{c.name}: demand must be positive")
        gap: float = beta * math.log(1.0 / c.p) + M + gamma - c.r
        if gap <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError(f"{c.name}: transport gap must be positive")
        ideal: float = gamma * c.d / gap
        service: float = grid_ceil(rho, ideal)
        out.append(Allocation(c.name, gap, ideal, service, service / ideal))
    return out

        assert a.service < rho * a.ideal, f"{a.name}: ceiling violated"
    tot_ideal: float = sum(a.ideal for a in allocations)
    tot_service: float = sum(a.service for a in allocations)
    return {
        "total_ideal": tot_ideal,
        "total_service": tot_service,
        "aggregate_slack": tot_service / tot_ideal,
        "max_slack": max(a.slack for a in allocations),
        "min_slack": min(a.slack for a in allocations),

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


def grid_cost(rho: float) -> float:
    """C(rho) = rho / log(rho), defined for rho > 1."""
    if rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("grid ratio must exceed 1")
    return rho / math.log(rho)


def typical_slack(rho: float) -> float:
    """Geometric-mean overshoot of the phase-jittered grid-rho arbiter: sqrt(rho)."""
    return math.sqrt(rho)

    """Arithmetic-mean overshoot of the jittered arbiter: (rho - 1)/log(rho)."""
    return (rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho)


def worst_case_slack(rho: float) -> float:
    """Supremum of the overshoot, approached but never attained: rho."""
    return rho

    typical: float
    mean: float
    worst: float
    cost: float
    excess_over_optimum: float


def report(rho: float) -> GridReport:
    """All four constants of a candidate grid ratio, plus its relative excess."""
    c = grid_cost(rho)

        rho=rho,
        typical=typical_slack(rho),
        mean=mean_slack(rho),
        worst=worst_case_slack(rho),
        cost=c,
        excess_over_optimum=c / math.e - 1.0,

def golden_section_min(f: Callable[[float], float], lo: float, hi: float,

    """Minimise a strictly unimodal f on [lo, hi]; O(iterations) evaluations."""
    inv_phi: float = (math.sqrt(5.0) - 1.0) / 2.0

import math
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def star_discrepancy(sample: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    d = 0.0
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        d = max(d, abs((i + 1) / n - x), abs(i / n - x))
    return d


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5))

      <div class="stat"><div class="k">min slack (floor 1)</div><div class="v" id="sMin">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">max slack (ceiling 2)</div><div class="v" id="sMax">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">star discrepancy</div><div class="v" id="sDisc">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">geometric mean</div><div class="v" id="sGeo">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">arithmetic mean</div><div class="v" id="sAri">–</div></div>
    </div>
    <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <details>
      <summary style="cursor:pointer;font-weight:600">Why the fractional part? (click to expand)</summary>
      <p style="line-height:1.6">
        The arbiter delivers 2<sup>⌈log₂x⌉</sup> for a request x, so the slack is
        2<sup>⌈log₂x⌉ − log₂x</sup>. For any real u one has ⌈u⌉ − u = {−u}, so the overshoot in
        backoff levels is exactly {−log₂x}. Putting x = α<sup>n</sup> gives {−n·log₂α}: consecutive
        rounds advance by a fixed angle on the circle ℝ/ℤ. If that angle is rational, p/q, the orbit
        closes after q steps and only q overshoot values ever occur. If it is irrational, the orbit
        never closes and — by Kronecker's theorem — comes arbitrarily close to every point of the
        circle, so the exchange eventually realises every slack in [1, 2), saturating both the
        no-starvation floor 1 and the unimprovable ceiling 2.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>

<script>
(function(){
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const alphaEl = $("alpha"), nEl = $("n");
  const circle = $("circle"), saw = $("saw"), hist = $("hist");

  // rational detection by continued fractions with a small denominator bound
  function rationalApprox(x, maxDen){
    let h1=1,h0=0,k1=0,k0=1,b=x;
    for(let i=0;i<30;i++){
      const a=Math.floor(b);
      let h2=a*h1+h0, k2=a*k1+k0;
      if(k2>maxDen) break;
      h0=h1;h1=h2;k0=k1;k1=k2;
      if(Math.abs(x-h1/k1) < 1e-12) return {p:h1,q:k1};
      const fr=b-a;
      if(fr<1e-14) break;
      b=1/fr;

    return null;
  }
  const frac = t => t - Math.floor(t);

  const aspect = new WeakMap();
  function setupCanvas(cv){
    if(!aspect.has(cv)) aspect.set(cv, cv.height/cv.width);
    const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio||1;
    const W = cv.clientWidth || 600;
    const H = W*aspect.get(cv);
    cv.width = Math.round(W*dpr);
    cv.height = Math.round(H*dpr);
    cv.style.height = H+"px";
    const ctx = cv.getContext("2d");
    ctx.setTransform(dpr,0,0,dpr,0,0);
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    return {ctx, W, H};
  }

  function starDiscrepancy(sorted){
    const n = sorted.length; let d=0;
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
      d = Math.max(d, Math.abs((i+1)/n - sorted[i]), Math.abs(i/n - sorted[i]));
    }
    return d;
  }

  function drawCircle(orbit){
    const {ctx,W,H} = setupCanvas(circle);
    const cx=W/2, cy=H/2, R=Math.min(W,H)*0.36;
    ctx.strokeStyle="#d8e2ec"; ctx.lineWidth=2;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx,cy,R,0,2*Math.PI); ctx.stroke();
    // ticks
    ctx.fillStyle="#5c7089"; ctx.font="12px system-ui"; ctx.textAlign="center";
    for(let k=0;k<4;k++){
      const t=k/4, a=-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*t;
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(cx+Math.cos(a)*(R-6), cy+Math.sin(a)*(R-6));
      ctx.lineTo(cx+Math.cos(a)*(R+6), cy+Math.sin(a)*(R+6));
      ctx.strokeStyle="#b9c8d8"; ctx.lineWidth=1.5; ctx.stroke();
      ctx.fillText(t.toFixed(2), cx+Math.cos(a)*(R+22), cy+Math.sin(a)*(R+26));
    }
    // orbit points, faded by age
    const n=orbit.length;
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
      const t=orbit[i], a=-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*t;
      const age = 1 - i/n;
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.fillStyle = `rgba(142,36,170,${0.16+0.7*age*age})`;
      ctx.arc(cx+Math.cos(a)*R, cy+Math.sin(a)*R, i<12?5.5:3.2, 0, 2*Math.PI);
      ctx.fill();
    }
    // first few chords to show the rotation step
    ctx.strokeStyle="rgba(31,78,121,.35)"; ctx.lineWidth=1.4;
    ctx.beginPath();
    for(let i=0;i<Math.min(12,n);i++){
      const a=-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*orbit[i];
      const x=cx+Math.cos(a)*R, y=cy+Math.sin(a)*R;
      if(i===0) ctx.moveTo(x,y); else ctx.lineTo(x,y);
    }
    ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillStyle="#12233a"; ctx.font="600 14px system-ui";
    ctx.fillText("rotation by −log₂α  on  ℝ/ℤ", cx, 26);
  }

  function drawSaw(orbit){
    const {ctx,W,H} = setupCanvas(saw);
    const L=54,Rr=18,T=34,B=44;
    const px = u => L + u*(W-L-Rr);
    const py = s => H-B - (s-0.95)/(2.12-0.95)*(H-T-B);
    ctx.strokeStyle="#eef3f8"; ctx.lineWidth=1;
    for(let s=1;s<=2.0001;s+=0.25){
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(s)); ctx.lineTo(W-Rr,py(s)); ctx.stroke();
    }
    // sawtooth
    ctx.strokeStyle="#1f4e79"; ctx.lineWidth=2.2; ctx.beginPath();
    for(let i=0;i<=400;i++){
      const u=i/400, s=Math.pow(2, frac(-u));
      const x=px(u), y=py(s);
      if(i===0) ctx.moveTo(x,y); else ctx.lineTo(x,y);
    }
    ctx.stroke();
    // floor / ceiling
    ctx.setLineDash([6,5]); ctx.lineWidth=1.6;
    ctx.strokeStyle="#2e7d32"; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(1)); ctx.lineTo(W-Rr,py(1)); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.strokeStyle="#c62828"; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(2)); ctx.lineTo(W-Rr,py(2)); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);
    // orbit points
    const n=orbit.length;
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
      const u=orbit[i], s=Math.pow(2,u);
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.fillStyle=`rgba(142,36,170,${0.18+0.7*(1-i/n)*(1-i/n)})`;
      ctx.arc(px(frac(-u)), py(s), i<12?5.5:3.2, 0, 2*Math.PI);
      ctx.fill();
    }
    ctx.fillStyle="#5c7089"; ctx.font="12px system-ui"; ctx.textAlign="right";
    ctx.fillText("2.0", L-8, py(2)+4); ctx.fillText("1.5", L-8, py(1.5)+4);
    ctx.fillText("1.0", L-8, py(1)+4);
    ctx.textAlign="center"; ctx.fillStyle="#12233a"; ctx.font="600 14px system-ui";
    ctx.fillText("slack = 2^{ −u }   (u = log₂ request  mod 1)", W/2, 22);
  }

  function drawHist(slacks){
    const {ctx,W,H} = setupCanvas(hist);
    const L=54,Rr=18,T=34,B=42, bins=60;
    const counts=new Array(bins).fill(0);
    slacks.forEach(s=>{
      let b=Math.floor((s-1)*bins); if(b<0)b=0; if(b>=bins)b=bins-1; counts[b]++;
    });
    const maxc=Math.max(1,...counts);
    const px = s => L + (s-1)*(W-L-Rr);
    const bw = (W-L-Rr)/bins;
    for(let b=0;b<bins;b++){
      const h=(counts[b]/maxc)*(H-T-B);
      ctx.fillStyle="rgba(142,36,170,.55)";
      ctx.fillRect(L+b*bw+0.6, H-B-h, bw-1.2, h);
    }
    // limiting density 1/(s log 2): expected count per bin = N * (1/bins) * density
    ctx.strokeStyle="#1f4e79"; ctx.lineWidth=2.2; ctx.beginPath();
    for(let i=0;i<=300;i++){
      const s = 1 + i/300;
      const expected = slacks.length*(1/bins)/(s*Math.log(2));
      const x = px(s), y = H-B-(expected/maxc)*(H-T-B);
      if(i===0) ctx.moveTo(x,y); else ctx.lineTo(x,y);
    }
    ctx.stroke();
    // mean markers
    const marks=[[Math.SQRT2,"#2e7d32","√2  geometric mean"],[1/Math.log(2),"#c62828","1/log 2  arithmetic mean"]];
    ctx.font="12px system-ui"; ctx.textAlign="left";
    marks.forEach(([v,c,lab],i)=>{
      ctx.strokeStyle=c; ctx.setLineDash([5,4]); ctx.lineWidth=1.6;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(px(v),T); ctx.lineTo(px(v),H-B); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.setLineDash([]); ctx.fillStyle=c;
      ctx.fillText(lab, px(v)+6, T+16+i*16);
    });
    ctx.fillStyle="#5c7089"; ctx.textAlign="center";
    [1,1.25,1.5,1.75,2].forEach(s=>ctx.fillText(s.toFixed(2), px(s), H-B+18));
    ctx.fillStyle="#12233a"; ctx.font="600 14px system-ui";
    ctx.fillText("empirical distribution of the slack over the observed rounds", W/2, 22);
  }

  function update(){
    const alpha = parseFloat(alphaEl.value);
    const N = parseInt(nEl.value,10);
    $("alphaLbl").textContent = alpha.toFixed(3);
    $("nLbl").textContent = N;
    const theta = Math.log2(alpha);
    const rat = rationalApprox(theta, 512);

    // In the rational case use exact modular arithmetic, so the finite orbit is
    // reported exactly instead of being smeared by floating-point drift.
    const exact = rat && Math.abs(theta-rat.p/rat.q)<1e-12;
    const orbit=[], slacks=[];
    for(let n=0;n<N;n++){
      const u = exact ? (((-n*rat.p) % rat.q) + rat.q) % rat.q / rat.q : frac(-n*theta);
      orbit.push(u); slacks.push(Math.pow(2,u));
    }
    drawCircle(orbit); drawSaw(orbit); drawHist(slacks);

    const rounded = new Set(orbit.map(u=>u.toFixed(7)));
    const sorted = orbit.slice().sort((a,b)=>a-b);
    const disc = starDiscrepancy(sorted);
    const geo = Math.exp(slacks.reduce((a,s)=>a+Math.log(s),0)/N);
    const ari = slacks.reduce((a,s)=>a+s,0)/N;
    $("sDistinct").textContent = rounded.size >= N ? N + " (all)" : rounded.size;
    $("sMin").textContent = Math.min(...slacks).toFixed(6);
    $("sMax").textContent = Math.max(...slacks).toFixed(6);
    $("sDisc").textContent = disc.toFixed(5);
    $("sGeo").textContent = geo.toFixed(5);
    $("sAri").textContent = ari.toFixed(5);

    const v=$("verdict");
    if(exact){
      v.className="verdict finite";
      v.innerHTML = `<b>log₂α = ${rat.p}/${rat.q} is rational.</b> The rotation closes after
        ${rat.q} step${rat.q>1?"s":""}: the orbit is periodic and this exchange will only ever see
        ${rat.q} distinct overshoot value${rat.q>1?"s":""}, no matter how long you watch.
        A finite set cannot be dense, so the factor-two ceiling is <i>never</i> approached
        ${rat.q===1?"— the slack is identically 1, perfect efficiency forever.":"."}`;
    } else {
      v.className="verdict dense";
      v.innerHTML = `<b>log₂α ≈ ${theta.toFixed(9)} has no small rational representation</b> — for
        α not a rational power of 2 it is genuinely irrational. The orbit never closes and is dense:
        given long enough, this single exchange realises <i>every</i> slack in [1, 2), coming
        arbitrarily close both to the no-starvation floor 1 and to the unimprovable ceiling 2.
        The star discrepancy above shrinks towards 0 as you increase N — that is equidistribution
        happening in front of you.`;
    }
  }

  alphaEl.addEventListener("input", ()=>{document.querySelectorAll(".presets button").forEach(b=>b.classList.remove("on"));update();});
  nEl.addEventListener("input", update);
  document.querySelectorAll(".presets button").forEach(b=>{
    b.addEventListener("click", ()=>{
      document.querySelectorAll(".presets button").forEach(x=>x.classList.remove("on"));
      b.classList.add("on");
      alphaEl.value = b.dataset.a; update();
    });
  });
  window.addEventListener("resize", update);
  update();
})();
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    },
    {
      "title": "The Backoff Design Bench: Worst Case, Typical Case, and the Price of a Grid",
      "description": "An interactive laboratory for the design constants. Three sliders control the grid ratio rho, the jitter phase theta and the ideal share x. The first panel draws the phase-shifted window ladder with the request and the delivered window highlighted and the resulting overshoot annotated, so the reader can watch a rung being chosen. The second panel plots the grid cost rho/log rho with the current ratio tracked, the optimum at Euler's number marked, and the exact tie between the binary and quaternary grids drawn as a level segment. The third panel sweeps the jitter phase across a full backoff level and plots the overshoot as a function of phase, with the typical constant sqrt(rho), the mean constant (rho-1)/log rho and the unattained worst case rho drawn as reference lines. The key lesson is kinesthetic: no matter where the phase slider is dragged, the overshoot stays inside [1, rho), so randomisation cannot improve the guarantee — it only reshapes the distribution. A collapsible section derives both averaged constants and proves the strict hierarchy between them.",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>The Backoff Design Bench — worst case, typical case, and the cost of a grid</title>
<style>
  :root{
    --ink:#12233a; --muted:#5c7089; --line:#d8e2ec; --bg:#f6f9fc;
    --accent:#1f4e79; --good:#2e7d32; --bad:#c62828; --pop:#8e24aa; --warm:#ef6c00;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
       font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Inter,Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif}

<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Backoff Design Bench</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    A grid-ρ arbiter allocates windows from the ladder … ρ⁻¹, 1, ρ, ρ², … and rounds every fair
    share <b>up</b> to the next rung. It therefore never starves a class, and it never overshoots by
    a factor of ρ or more. Randomising the ladder by a phase θ leaves both of those guarantees
    exactly as they were — but it fixes the <i>typical</i> overshoot at √ρ and the <i>average</i>
    overshoot at (ρ−1)/log ρ. Slide ρ and θ and watch all three constants move.
  </p>

  <div class="card">
    <div class="controls">
      <div>
        <label>grid ratio ρ = <span class="val" id="rhoLbl">2.000</span></label>

      <div>

        <input type="range" id="th" min="0" max="0.999" step="0.001" value="0">
      </div>
      <div>

        <span class="sw" style="background:var(--warm)"></span>the window actually delivered.
      </div>
    </div>

      <div class="legend">
