        one backoff level. Its unique minimum is at ρ = e, and C(4) = C(2) exactly.
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <canvas id="sweep" width="1400" height="360"></canvas>
    <div class="stats">
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">slack at this phase</div><div class="v" id="sNow">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">typical  √ρ</div><div class="v" id="sGeo">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">mean  (ρ−1)/log ρ</div><div class="v" id="sAri">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">worst case  ρ</div><div class="v" id="sSup">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">grid cost  C(ρ)</div><div class="v" id="sCost">–</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">excess over the optimum e</div><div class="v" id="sExc">–</div></div>
    </div>
    <div class="note" id="note"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <details>
      <summary>Where do √ρ and (ρ−1)/log ρ come from? (click to expand)</summary>
      <p>
        With phase θ the arbiter delivers ρ<sup>⌈log_ρ x − θ⌉ + θ</sup>, so the overshoot measured in
        backoff levels is exactly the fractional part {θ − log_ρ x}. As θ sweeps a unit interval that
        quantity sweeps the circle uniformly, so its average is ½ — whatever the request x, and
        whatever the exchange. Exponentiating, the geometric-mean overshoot is ρ<sup>1/2</sup> = √ρ.
        The arithmetic mean instead averages ρ<sup>s</sup> over s uniform on [0,1], which is
        ∫₀¹ ρ<sup>s</sup> ds = (ρ − 1)/log ρ.
      </p>
      <p>
        These two are always strictly ordered below the worst case:
        √ρ < (ρ−1)/log ρ < ρ. The left-hand gap is a strict arithmetic–geometric mean
        inequality; substituting u = √ρ turns it into 2 log u < u − 1/u, and the function
        u − 1/u − 2 log u vanishes at u = 1 with derivative (1 − 1/u)², a perfect square.
      </p>
      <p>
        Note what randomising does <i>not</i> do: the bound 1 ≤ slack < ρ holds at
        <b>every</b> phase, so no distribution over phases can lower the worst case. Randomisation
        buys a better typical case, never a better guarantee.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const rhoEl=$("rho"), thEl=$("th"), xEl=$("x");
  const E = Math.E;

  const aspect = new WeakMap();
  function setupCanvas(cv){
    if(!aspect.has(cv)) aspect.set(cv, cv.height/cv.width);
    const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio||1;
    const W = cv.clientWidth || 600, H = W*aspect.get(cv);
    cv.width=Math.round(W*dpr); cv.height=Math.round(H*dpr); cv.style.height=H+"px";
    const ctx=cv.getContext("2d"); ctx.setTransform(dpr,0,0,dpr,0,0); ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    return {ctx,W,H};
  }
  const logb = (b,z) => Math.log(z)/Math.log(b);
  function jitterCeil(rho, theta, x){
    return Math.pow(rho, Math.ceil(logb(rho,x)-theta)+theta);
  }

  function drawLadder(rho, theta, x){
    const {ctx,W,H} = setupCanvas($("ladder"));
    const T=40,B=46,L=58,R=22;
    const lo=-2.4, hi=2.4;                       // in units of log_rho
    const py = u => H-B - (u-lo)/(hi-lo)*(H-T-B);
    ctx.strokeStyle="#eef3f8"; ctx.lineWidth=1;
    // ladder rungs
    ctx.font="12px system-ui"; ctx.textAlign="right";
    for(let k=Math.ceil(lo);k<=Math.floor(hi);k++){
      const u=k+theta;
      if(u<lo||u>hi) continue;
      ctx.strokeStyle="#1f4e79"; ctx.lineWidth=2; ctx.globalAlpha=.55;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(u)); ctx.lineTo(W-R,py(u)); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.globalAlpha=1; ctx.fillStyle="#5c7089";
      ctx.fillText("ρ^"+(k+(theta?"+θ":"")), L-8, py(u)+4);
    }
    const ux = logb(rho,x);
    const win = jitterCeil(rho,theta,x), uw = logb(rho,win);
    // request
    ctx.strokeStyle="#8e24aa"; ctx.lineWidth=3;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(ux)); ctx.lineTo(W-R,py(ux)); ctx.stroke();
    // delivered window highlighted
    ctx.strokeStyle="#ef6c00"; ctx.lineWidth=4;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(uw)); ctx.lineTo(W-R,py(uw)); ctx.stroke();
    // the gap
    const xm=(L+W-R)/2;
    ctx.strokeStyle="#12233a"; ctx.lineWidth=1.5; ctx.setLineDash([4,4]);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(xm,py(ux)); ctx.lineTo(xm,py(uw)); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);
    ctx.fillStyle="#12233a"; ctx.textAlign="left"; ctx.font="600 13px system-ui";
    ctx.fillText("overshoot = "+(win/x).toFixed(4)+"×", xm+10, (py(ux)+py(uw))/2+4);

# The Floor Is Sharp

## A scheduler that promises never to starve anyone — and the exact price of keeping that promise

Imagine one optical fibre carrying many streams at once. Some are robust; nearly every photon
they send arrives. Others are fragile — a rare quantum channel where only one attempt in a
thousand succeeds. An arbiter at the head of the fibre must divide time between them, and it
makes a promise: **no stream will ever be starved.**

Concretely, class $y$ is entitled to its *ideal share*

$$\text{ideal}(y) \;=\; \frac{\gamma\, d(y)}{\beta \log(1/p(y)) + M + \gamma - r(y)},$$

where $p(y)\in(0,1]$ is the class's **occupancy** (probability that a slot given to it is
usable), $d(y)>0$ its **demand**, $r(y)$ a **reservation credit** it already holds, and
$\beta,\gamma,M$ are global constants — an inverse temperature, a scheduling quantum and a
background cost. The denominator is the *transport gap*: the Boltzmann cost of one successful
transfer, discounted by the class's credit. Rare channels have a big gap and a small share.

But a real arbiter cannot hand out arbitrary real numbers of microseconds. It hands out
**backoff windows**, and backoff windows come in powers of two. Faced with a fair share of
$1.3$, it must deliver $2$.

$$\text{service}(y) \;=\; 2^{\lceil \log_2 \text{ideal}(y)\rceil}.$$

The promise is kept — rounding *up* can only be generous. The question of this page is: **how
generous, exactly?**

---

## 1. First contact: the sawtooth

Everything follows from one picture. Write the request size on a logarithmic scale. Rounding up
to the next power of two produces an overshoot that drops to $1$ exactly on the grid and then
climbs back towards — but never reaches — $2$. It is a sawtooth of period one, and its range is
the half-open interval $[1,2)$: closed at the bottom, open at the top, forever.

{{visualization:0}}

Panel (a) is the sawtooth. Panel (b) is the twist we will spend the rest of the page on: what
happens when a single exchange's demand *grows*, so it samples this sawtooth round after round.
Panel (c) is the distribution those samples converge to.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to see why the range is exactly $[1,2)$ — and why the top is never attained</b></summary>

Two one-line facts about $\mathrm{gridCeil}(x) = 2^{\lceil \log_2 x\rceil}$:

* **Covering.** $\lceil t\rceil \ge t$, so $2^{\lceil \log_2 x\rceil} \ge 2^{\log_2 x} = x$.
  Nobody is starved.
* **Efficiency.** $\lceil t\rceil < t+1$, so $2^{\lceil \log_2 x\rceil} < 2^{\log_2 x + 1} = 2x$.
  Nobody is over-served by a factor of two.

For sharpness one needs a witness. Take the one-class exchange with $\beta=\gamma=M=1$,
a perfect channel $p\equiv 1$ (so $\log(1/p)=0$) and credit $r\equiv 1$. Its gap is
$0+1+1-1=1$, so its ideal share is just its demand $x$. Now the key observation: on the whole
interval $1 < x \le 2$ the arbiter must jump all the way to the window $2$, so the overshoot is
$2/x$. Letting $x$ run over $(1,2]$ makes $2/x$ run over the whole of $[1,2)$.

**Theorem (slack spectrum).** *The set of achievable ratios $\mathrm{service}/\mathrm{ideal}$
over all exchanges is exactly $[1,2)$.*

The value $1$ is attained (demand exactly $1$, already a power of two) and $2$ is the exact
supremum, never reached. Structurally, this is because the overshoot is **log-periodic**:
scaling the demand by $2$ scales the window by $2$, so the overshoot is unchanged, and one
period of the sawtooth is the decreasing map $x\mapsto 2/x$ on $(1,2]$.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Click to see why the constant is the grid ratio and nothing else</b></summary>

Replace the ladder $2^{\mathbb Z}$ by $\rho^{\mathbb Z}$ for any $\rho > 1$. Then, for every real
constant $c$:

$$\big(\forall \text{ exchanges}: \mathrm{service}_\rho \le c\cdot \mathrm{ideal}\big)
\iff \rho \le c,
\qquad
\big(\forall \text{ exchanges}: c\cdot \mathrm{ideal} \le \mathrm{service}_\rho\big)
\iff c \le 1.$$

Both directions are one line given the witness family: the "if" halves are the covering and
efficiency lemmas, and the "only if" halves are the witness with demand $\rho/t$, which realises
overshoot exactly $t$ for any $t\in[1,\rho)$.

So the famous "factor of two" in backoff analysis is not slack in the analysis. It is the width
of the grid. Both bounds also survive summation over a finite family of classes: the whole
channel pays the same factor, no more.
</details>

---

## 2. Playing with the arbiter: worst case, typical case, and the cost of a grid

A natural engineering instinct: if deterministic rounding costs a factor of two, **randomise**.
Shift the whole ladder by a random phase $\theta$, delivering
$\rho^{\lceil \log_\rho x - \theta\rceil + \theta}$.

Try it. Slide the phase and watch the guarantee refuse to move.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

The bound $1 \le \text{slack} < \rho$ holds at *every* phase, so no distribution over phases can
lower the worst case. That popular conjecture is simply false. What randomisation *does* change
is the distribution: the overshoot, measured in backoff levels, is exactly the fractional part
$\{\theta - \log_\rho x\}$, which sweeps the circle uniformly as $\theta$ sweeps $[0,1)$. Hence

$$\text{typical (geometric mean)} = \sqrt{\rho},
\qquad
\text{average (arithmetic mean)} = \frac{\rho-1}{\log \rho},$$

both independent of the request and of the exchange. For $\rho=2$: $1.4142 < 1.4427 < 2$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for the proof of the strict hierarchy $\sqrt\rho < (\rho-1)/\log\rho < \rho$</b></summary>

*Left inequality.* Put $u = \sqrt\rho > 1$. The claim becomes $2\log u < u - 1/u$. Let
$f(u) = u - 1/u - 2\log u$. Then $f(1) = 0$ and

$$f'(u) = 1 + \frac{1}{u^2} - \frac{2}{u} = \Big(1 - \frac{1}{u}\Big)^2 > 0 \quad (u > 1),$$

a perfect square. So $f$ is strictly increasing and positive for $u>1$. (This inequality was
first spotted in the numerics and only afterwards given this proof.)

*Right inequality.* Apply $\log t < t-1$ with $t = 1/\rho$: $-\log\rho < 1/\rho - 1$, i.e.
$\log\rho > (\rho-1)/\rho$, i.e. $(\rho-1)/\log\rho < \rho$.
</details>

### So why does everyone use $\rho = 2$?

Because a bigger grid costs more per round but covers more dynamic range per level. The honest
figure of merit is the **grid cost** $C(\rho) = \rho/\log\rho$. Minimise it and you get a
surprise: the answer is not $2$, it is **Euler's number**.

$$e \le \frac{\rho}{\log \rho} \quad\text{for all } \rho>1, \quad\text{with equality only at }
\rho = e.$$

The proof is the tangent-line bound $\log t \le t-1$ at $t=\rho/e$. And two arithmetic curios:
$C(4) = 4/(2\log 2) = 2/\log 2 = C(2)$ — binary and quaternary backoff cost **exactly** the same,
which makes doubling a fixed point of the design trade-off — while the dyadic grid sits just
$6.15\%$ above the theoretical optimum. Among integer ratios, $3$ is the best, within half a
percent of $e$.

{{visualization:1}}

{{algorithm:2}}

## 3. The twist: one exchange, watched long enough, sees everything

Everything above quantifies over the *space* of exchanges. Sharpness meant: somewhere in the
design space there is a configuration with overshoot near $2$. That is a statement about a
designer's freedom, not about a running system.

Here is the sharper question. Fix one exchange and let it run, with demand growing by a factor
$\alpha$ per round, so the ideal share climbs the ladder $\alpha^n$. Take logarithms:

$$\log_2 \text{slack}(\alpha^n) \;=\; \{-n\log_2 \alpha\}.$$

That is the orbit of a **rotation of the circle** $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ by the angle
$-\log_2\alpha$. And circle rotations obey one of the oldest dichotomies in mathematics.

**Play with it.** Set $\alpha=3$ and watch the dots fill the circle; set $\alpha=4$ and watch
them collapse to a single point; set $\alpha=\sqrt2$ and get two; set $\alpha=2^{3/7}$ and get
seven. Then watch the discrepancy readout: it shrinks to zero exactly when the orbit is dense.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

**Theorem (Diophantine dichotomy).** *For $\alpha>0$, the overshoot orbit of the geometric
demand ladder is dense in the full spectrum if and only if $\log_2\alpha$ is irrational.*

<details>
<summary><b>Click for both halves of the proof</b></summary>

*Irrational $\Rightarrow$ dense (Kronecker).* The additive subgroup of $\mathbb R$ generated by
$\vartheta$ and $1$ is dense exactly when $\vartheta\notin\mathbb Q$ — a closed subgroup of
$\mathbb R$ is either cyclic or everything, and cyclicity would force $\vartheta$ rational. Given
a target $y\in(0,1)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta = \min(\varepsilon,y,1-y)$ and a group
element $z = m\vartheta + k$ with $|z-y|<\delta$. Then $0<z<1$, so $\{m\vartheta\} = z$, and we
have approximated $y$ to within $\varepsilon$.

*Rational $\Rightarrow$ finite.* If $\log_2\alpha = p/q$ then
$\{(n+kq)(-p/q)\} = \{n(-p/q) - kp\} = \{n(-p/q)\}$: the orbit is periodic with period $q$ and
takes at most $q$ values. A finite set is closed and cannot be dense in an interval.

*Quantitatively, in the dense case:* for every $0<\varepsilon<1$ some round has overshoot
exceeding $2^{1-\varepsilon}$ and some round has overshoot below $2^{\varepsilon}$. One exchange
saturates **both** ends of the spectrum, all by itself.
</details>

And it is easy to be on the dense side. $\log_2\alpha$ is irrational whenever $\alpha$ is not a
rational power of $2$. For $\alpha = 3$: if $\log_2 3 = p/q$ then $3^q = 2^p$, an odd number
equal to an even one. So a stream that **triples** each round will eventually waste almost a full
factor of two — and, on other rounds, be served with essentially perfect efficiency. A stream
that **quadruples** sits on the grid forever, overshoot exactly $1$, never wasting a slot.

{{algorithm:1}}

The dichotomy is qualitative, but the waiting times are perfectly concrete: for ternary growth
the first round with overshoot above $1.99$ arrives at $n=53$, and above $1.999$ at $n=665$.

## 5. What to take away

* The promise — nobody is starved — is exactly right, and the price of keeping it with a
  physically realisable arbiter is **exactly the grid ratio**: overshoot in $[1,\rho)$, both
  constants optimal.
* Randomising the grid **cannot** improve the guarantee. It sets the typical cost at $\sqrt\rho$
  and the average cost at $(\rho-1)/\log\rho$, strictly below $\rho$ and strictly ordered.
* The best possible grid ratio is $e$; $2$ costs $6.15\%$ more and ties exactly with $4$.
* Whether a *particular running system* ever feels the worst case is decided by a question in
  number theory: dense overshoot if and only if $\log_2$ of its growth rate is irrational.

Between "eventually meets every inefficiency the design permits" and "never wastes a single
slot" lies nothing but the difference between an irrational number and a rational one — a fact
about arithmetic, quietly governing a fact about photons.

# PTX transport: the no-starvation floor and its sharp factor `2`

## The physical model

A *photon-transport exchange* (PTX) is an idealised model of a shared quantum channel that
multiplexes several transport classes `y`.  Each class is described by three numbers:

* `p y ∈ (0,1]` — the *occupancy* (the probability that a slot offered to `y` is actually
  usable);
* `d y > 0`    — the *demand* (how much channel time class `y` asks for);
* `r y`        — the *reservation credit* already granted to `y` by the arbiter.

Three global constants govern the exchange: an inverse temperature `β > 0`, a scheduling
quantum `γ > 0`, and a background cost `M`.

The **transport gap** of class `y` is the Boltzmann cost of one successful transfer, corrected
by the class's own credit,
```
gap y  =  β · log (1 / p y)  +  M  +  γ  −  r y ,
```
and the **ideal service** that a perfectly divisible arbiter would hand to `y` is
```
ideal y  =  γ · d y / gap y .
```
This is the familiar "`γ d / (β log(1/p) + M + γ − r)`" expression: a rare class
(`p y` small, hence `log (1/p y)` large) has a large gap and therefore a small ideal share,
while a class holding a large credit `r y` has a small gap and a large share.

A *real* arbiter cannot hand out an arbitrary real amount of channel time.  Slots are handed
out in **binary exponential backoff windows**: the arbiter must pick a window that is an
integer power of two (positive or negative) of the base quantum, and it picks the smallest
such window that covers the ideal share.  Hence the delivered service is
```
service y  =  2 ^ ⌈log₂ (ideal y)⌉ .
```

## What is proved here

* `ptx_no_starvation` : `ideal y ≤ service y` — the floor.  No class is ever starved: it always
  receives at least `γ d y / (β log (1/p y) + M + γ − r y)`.
* `ptx_service_lt_two_ideal` : `service y < 2 · ideal y` — the ceiling, valid for *every*
  instance.  In particular there really are instances with `service y ≤ 2 · ideal y`, which is
  the statement that the floor cannot be improved by more than a factor of `2`.
* `ptx_floor_attained` : an explicit instance with `service y = ideal y`.  Consequently
  (`ptx_floor_constant_optimal`) the constant `1` in the floor is *exactly* optimal: no
  `c > 1` works uniformly.
* `ptx_ratio_approaches_two` : for every `ε > 0` an instance whose slack exceeds `2 − ε`.
  Together with the ceiling this pins the supremum of the slack at exactly `2`
  (`ptx_two_is_optimal_ceiling`): the "factor `2`" in the headline statement is not an
  artefact of the proof, it is the exact width of the dyadic backoff grid.

The technical engine is the *grid quantiser* `gridCeil ρ x = ρ ^ ⌈log_ρ x⌉`, developed for a
general ratio `ρ > 1` in the first section; the value `ρ = 2` of the PTX arbiter is what
produces the factor `2`.
-/

import Mathlib

namespace Physics.PTX

open Real

/-! ## 1. The grid quantiser -/

/-- `gridCeil ρ x` is the smallest power of `ρ` (integer exponent, possibly negative) that is
at least `x`.  For `ρ = 2` this is the binary exponential backoff window covering `x`. -/
noncomputable def gridCeil (rho x : ℝ) : ℝ := rho ^ (⌈Real.logb rho x⌉ : ℤ)

lemma gridCeil_pos {rho x : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) : 0 < gridCeil rho x :=
  zpow_pos (lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho) _

lemma gridCeil_eq_rpow {rho x : ℝ} :
    gridCeil rho x = rho ^ ((⌈Real.logb rho x⌉ : ℤ) : ℝ) := by
  rw [gridCeil, Real.rpow_intCast]

/-- **Covering property.** The quantised window is never smaller than the request. -/
lemma self_le_gridCeil {rho x : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) (hx : 0 < x) : x ≤ gridCeil rho x := by
  have h0 : (0 : ℝ) < rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho
  have hlog : rho ^ (Real.logb rho x) = x := Real.rpow_logb h0 (ne_of_gt hrho) hx
  calc x = rho ^ (Real.logb rho x) := hlog.symm
    _ ≤ rho ^ ((⌈Real.logb rho x⌉ : ℤ) : ℝ) :=
        Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_le (le_of_lt hrho) (Int.le_ceil _)
    _ = gridCeil rho x := gridCeil_eq_rpow.symm

/-- **Efficiency property.** The quantised window overshoots by strictly less than the grid
ratio `ρ`. -/
lemma gridCeil_lt {rho x : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) (hx : 0 < x) : gridCeil rho x < rho * x := by
  have h0 : (0 : ℝ) < rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho
  have hlog : rho ^ (Real.logb rho x) = x := Real.rpow_logb h0 (ne_of_gt hrho) hx
  have hceil : ((⌈Real.logb rho x⌉ : ℤ) : ℝ) < Real.logb rho x + 1 := Int.ceil_lt_add_one _
  calc gridCeil rho x = rho ^ ((⌈Real.logb rho x⌉ : ℤ) : ℝ) := gridCeil_eq_rpow
    _ < rho ^ (Real.logb rho x + 1) := (Real.rpow_lt_rpow_left_iff hrho).2 hceil
    _ = rho ^ (Real.logb rho x) * rho := by rw [Real.rpow_add h0, Real.rpow_one]
    _ = x * rho := by rw [hlog]
    _ = rho * x := mul_comm _ _

/-- On the half-open interval `(1, ρ]` the quantiser must jump all the way to `ρ`. -/
lemma gridCeil_eq_base_of_mem_Ioc {rho x : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) (hx1 : 1 < x) (hx2 : x ≤ rho) :
    gridCeil rho x = rho := by
  have h0 : (0 : ℝ) < rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho
  have hx0 : (0 : ℝ) < x := lt_trans zero_lt_one hx1
  have hlogpos : 0 < Real.logb rho x := Real.logb_pos hrho hx1
  have hlogle : Real.logb rho x ≤ 1 := by
    rw [Real.logb_le_iff_le_rpow hrho hx0, Real.rpow_one]
    exact hx2
  have hceil : ⌈Real.logb rho x⌉ = (1 : ℤ) := by
    rw [Int.ceil_eq_iff]
    constructor
    · push_cast; linarith
    · push_cast; linarith
  rw [gridCeil, hceil, zpow_one]

/-- A photon-transport exchange: global constants `β, γ, M` together with occupancies `p`,
demands `d` and reservation credits `r` for each transport class. -/
structure PTXInstance (ι : Type*) where
  beta : ℝ
  gamma : ℝ
  M : ℝ
  p : ι → ℝ
  d : ι → ℝ
  r : ι → ℝ
  beta_pos : 0 < beta
  gamma_pos : 0 < gamma
  p_pos : ∀ y, 0 < p y
  p_le_one : ∀ y, p y ≤ 1
  d_pos : ∀ y, 0 < d y
  gap_pos : ∀ y, 0 < beta * Real.log (1 / p y) + M + gamma - r y

noncomputable def gap (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : ℝ :=
  I.beta * Real.log (1 / I.p y) + I.M + I.gamma - I.r y

/-- The ideal (perfectly divisible) share `γ d y / gap y` of class `y`. -/
noncomputable def ideal (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : ℝ := I.gamma * I.d y / gap I y

/-- The service actually delivered by the dyadic backoff arbiter. -/
noncomputable def service (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : ℝ := gridCeil 2 (ideal I y)

lemma gap_pos' (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : 0 < gap I y := I.gap_pos y

lemma ideal_pos (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : 0 < ideal I y :=
  div_pos (mul_pos I.gamma_pos (I.d_pos y)) (gap_pos' I y)

  gridCeil_pos (by norm_num)

smaller Boltzmann cost.  (Both classes are compared inside the same exchange.) -/
lemma gap_antitone_in_p (I : PTXInstance ι) {y z : ι}
    (hp : I.p y ≤ I.p z) (hMr : I.M - I.r y = I.M - I.r z) : gap I z ≤ gap I y := by
  have hpy : 0 < I.p y := I.p_pos y
  have hpz : 0 < I.p z := I.p_pos z
  have h : Real.log (1 / I.p z) ≤ Real.log (1 / I.p y) := by
    apply Real.log_le_log (by positivity)
    exact one_div_le_one_div_of_le hpy hp
  have := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left h (le_of_lt I.beta_pos)
  simp only [gap]
  linarith [hMr]

`γ d y / (β log (1/p y) + M + γ − r y)` units of channel time. -/
theorem ptx_no_starvation (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) :
    I.gamma * I.d y / (I.beta * Real.log (1 / I.p y) + I.M + I.gamma - I.r y) ≤ service I y :=
  self_le_gridCeil (by norm_num) (ideal_pos I y)

noncomputable def jitterCeil (rho theta x : ℝ) : ℝ :=

  have he : Real.logb rho x ≤ ((⌈Real.logb rho x - theta⌉ : ℤ) : ℝ) + theta := by
    have := Int.le_ceil (Real.logb rho x - theta)
    linarith

    _ ≤ rho ^ (((⌈Real.logb rho x - theta⌉ : ℤ) : ℝ) + theta) :=
        Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_le (le_of_lt hrho) he
    _ = jitterCeil rho theta x := rfl

  have hlog : rho ^ (Real.logb rho x) = x := Real.rpow_logb h0 (ne_of_gt hrho) hx
  have he : ((⌈Real.logb rho x - theta⌉ : ℤ) : ℝ) + theta < Real.logb rho x + 1 := by

    _ = rho ^ (Real.logb rho x) * rho := by rw [Real.rpow_add h0, Real.rpow_one]
    _ = rho * x := by rw [hlog]; ring

    integral_comp_fract_unit (fun u => rho ^ u), integral_rpow_const hrho]

theorem ptx_dyadic_mean_slack {x : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) :
    ∫ theta in (0:ℝ)..1, jitterCeil 2 theta x / x = 1 / Real.log 2 := by
  rw [jitter_arithmetic_mean_slack (by norm_num) hx]
  norm_num

  nlinarith [Real.sq_sqrt (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ≤ 2), Real.sqrt_nonneg 2]

theorem ptx_dyadic_jitter_gain {x : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) :

  rw [jitter_geometric_mean_slack (by norm_num) hx]
  exact sqrt_two_lt_two

  have h0 : (0:ℝ) < rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho

  have hspos : 0 < Real.sqrt rho := Real.sqrt_pos.2 h0
  nlinarith [hs, hspos, hrho]

noncomputable def serviceJitter {ι : Type*} (rho theta : ℝ) (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : ℝ :=

theorem ptx_jitter_no_starvation {ι : Type*} {rho theta : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho)

  self_le_jitterCeil hrho (ideal_pos I y)

  jitterCeil_lt (by norm_num) (ideal_pos I y)

/-- `2 log u < u − 1/u` for `u > 1`: the derivative of `u − 1/u − 2 log u` is the perfect square

        have h1 : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => t) 1 t := hasDerivAt_id t
        have h2 : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => 1 / t) (-(1 / t ^ 2)) t := by
          simpa using hasDerivAt_inv (ne_of_gt ht0)
        have h3 : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => Real.log t) (1 / t) t := by
          simpa using Real.hasDerivAt_log (ne_of_gt ht0)
        exact (h1.sub h2).sub (h3.const_mul 2)
      rw [hd.deriv]
      have heq : 1 - (-(1 / t ^ 2)) - 2 * (1 / t) = (1 - 1 / t) ^ 2 := by field_simp; ring
      rw [heq]
      have hlt : 1 / t < 1 := by rw [div_lt_one ht0]; exact ht1
      have : 0 < 1 - 1 / t := by linarith
      positivity
  have h := key (le_refl (1:ℝ)) (le_of_lt hu) hu
  simp only [Real.log_one] at h
  norm_num at h
  rw [one_div]
  exact h

/-- **The typical slack is strictly below the mean slack, for every grid ratio.**  This is the
strict AM–GM gap `√ρ < (ρ − 1)/log ρ`. -/
theorem sqrt_lt_mean_slack {rho : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) :
    Real.sqrt rho < (rho - 1) / Real.log rho := by
  have h0 : (0:ℝ) < rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho
  have hs : 1 < Real.sqrt rho := by
    rw [show (1:ℝ) = Real.sqrt 1 by simp]
    exact Real.sqrt_lt_sqrt (by norm_num) hrho
  have hsq : Real.sqrt rho * Real.sqrt rho = rho := Real.mul_self_sqrt (le_of_lt h0)
  have hspos : 0 < Real.sqrt rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hs
  have hlogpos : 0 < Real.log rho := Real.log_pos hrho
  have hlog : 2 * Real.log (Real.sqrt rho) = Real.log rho := by
    rw [show (2:ℝ) * Real.log (Real.sqrt rho)
        = Real.log (Real.sqrt rho) + Real.log (Real.sqrt rho) by ring,
      ← Real.log_mul (ne_of_gt hspos) (ne_of_gt hspos), hsq]
  have hkey := two_log_lt_sub_inv hs
  rw [hlog] at hkey
  rw [lt_div_iff₀ hlogpos]
  have hinv : Real.sqrt rho - 1 / Real.sqrt rho = (rho - 1) / Real.sqrt rho := by
    field_simp
    nlinarith [hsq]
  rw [hinv, lt_div_iff₀ hspos] at hkey
  nlinarith [hkey, hsq, hspos, hlogpos]

  have hlogpos : 0 < Real.log rho := Real.log_pos hrho

      linarith)

  rw [div_lt_iff₀ hlogpos]
  have hmul : rho * (1 / rho) = 1 := by field_simp
  nlinarith [hinv, hmul]

/-- **The three constants of a grid-`ρ` arbiter are strictly ordered**: typical `√ρ`, mean
`(ρ−1)/log ρ`, worst case `ρ`. -/
theorem ptx_slack_constant_hierarchy {rho : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) :
    Real.sqrt rho < (rho - 1) / Real.log rho ∧ (rho - 1) / Real.log rho < rho :=
  ⟨sqrt_lt_mean_slack hrho, mean_slack_lt_worst_case hrho⟩

/-! ## 3. The optimal grid ratio is `e`, and `2` is within 7 % of it -/

noncomputable def gridCost (rho : ℝ) : ℝ := rho / Real.log rho

/-- **Euler's number is a lower bound for the grid cost.** -/
theorem exp_one_le_gridCost {rho : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) : Real.exp 1 ≤ gridCost rho := by
  have hlogpos : 0 < Real.log rho := Real.log_pos hrho
  have he : (0:ℝ) < Real.exp 1 := Real.exp_pos 1
  have hkey : Real.log rho ≤ rho / Real.exp 1 := by
    have hpos : 0 < rho / Real.exp 1 := div_pos (lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho) he
    have h := Real.log_le_sub_one_of_pos hpos
    rw [Real.log_div (by positivity) (ne_of_gt he), Real.log_exp] at h
    linarith
  rw [gridCost, le_div_iff₀ hlogpos]

        exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hkey (le_of_lt he)
    _ = rho := by field_simp

theorem gridCost_exp_one : gridCost (Real.exp 1) = Real.exp 1 := by
  rw [gridCost, Real.log_exp, div_one]

/-- **Uniqueness of the optimum.**  Any grid ratio other than `e` is strictly worse. -/
theorem exp_one_lt_gridCost_of_ne {rho : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) (hne : rho ≠ Real.exp 1) :
    Real.exp 1 < gridCost rho := by
  have hlogpos : 0 < Real.log rho := Real.log_pos hrho
  have he : (0:ℝ) < Real.exp 1 := Real.exp_pos 1
  have hpos : 0 < rho / Real.exp 1 := div_pos (lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho) he
  have hne1 : rho / Real.exp 1 ≠ 1 := by
    intro h
    exact hne (by field_simp at h; exact h)
  have h := Real.log_lt_sub_one_of_pos hpos hne1
  rw [Real.log_div (by positivity) (ne_of_gt he), Real.log_exp] at h
  have hkey : Real.log rho < rho / Real.exp 1 := by linarith
  rw [gridCost, lt_div_iff₀ hlogpos]
  calc Real.exp 1 * Real.log rho < Real.exp 1 * (rho / Real.exp 1) := by
        exact mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left hkey he
    _ = rho := by field_simp

cost is invariant under squaring the ratio only at these two points, which is why doubling the
window size is a fixed point of the design trade-off. -/

`Physics.PTXStarvationFloor` established the two-sided estimate

```
ideal y  ≤  service y  <  2 · ideal y ,      ideal y = γ d y / (β log(1/p y) + M + γ − r y),
```

slack ratios that occur, and identifies where the constant `2` comes from.

* `ptx_slack_mem_Ico` : the slack `service y / ideal y` always lies in `[1, 2)`.

  scaling the demand by the grid ratio, i.e. it is log-periodic with period `log ρ`.  This is
  the structural reason the supremum `ρ` is never attained: the slack orbit is a scale-invariant
  half-open interval.

/-! ## 1. Structural properties of the quantiser -/

/-- Scaling the request by the grid ratio scales the quantised window by the grid ratio:
the arbiter is equivariant for the multiplicative action of `ρ^ℤ`. -/
lemma gridCeil_mul_base {rho x : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) (hx : 0 < x) :
    gridCeil rho (rho * x) = rho * gridCeil rho x := by
  have h0 : (0 : ℝ) < rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho
  have hlog : Real.logb rho (rho * x) = Real.logb rho x + 1 := by
    rw [Real.logb_mul (ne_of_gt h0) (ne_of_gt hx), Real.logb_self_eq_one hrho]
    ring
  rw [gridCeil, gridCeil, hlog, Int.ceil_add_one, zpow_add₀ (ne_of_gt h0), zpow_one]
  ring

/-- The quantiser is monotone. -/
lemma gridCeil_mono {rho x y : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) (hx : 0 < x) (hxy : x ≤ y) :
    gridCeil rho x ≤ gridCeil rho y := by
  have h0 : (0 : ℝ) < rho := lt_trans zero_lt_one hrho
  have hy : 0 < y := lt_of_lt_of_le hx hxy
  have hlog : Real.logb rho x ≤ Real.logb rho y := (Real.logb_le_logb hrho hx hy).2 hxy
  have hceil : ⌈Real.logb rho x⌉ ≤ ⌈Real.logb rho y⌉ := Int.ceil_le_ceil hlog
  exact zpow_le_zpow_right₀ (le_of_lt hrho) hceil

theorem ptx_slack_mem_Ico (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) :

  · rw [div_lt_iff₀ hpos]

/-- The service delivered by an arbiter whose backoff windows form the grid `ρ^ℤ`. -/
noncomputable def serviceGrid (rho : ℝ) (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : ℝ :=
  gridCeil rho (ideal I y)

@[simp] lemma serviceGrid_two (I : PTXInstance ι) (y : ι) : serviceGrid 2 I y = service I y := rfl

  gridCeil_lt hrho (ideal_pos I y)

theorem ptx_grid_optimal_ceiling_iff {rho : ℝ} (hrho : 1 < rho) (c : ℝ) :

  · intro hc I y

      by the witness exchange with demand 2/t, and nothing outside [1,2) occurs;
  3.  the optimal constants for a general grid ratio rho are 1 and rho;
  4.  aggregation:  sum(ideal) <= sum(service) < 2 * sum(ideal);
  5.  jitter:  the floor and ceiling hold at every phase, the geometric-mean
      slack is sqrt(rho) and the arithmetic-mean slack is (rho-1)/log(rho),
      with the strict hierarchy sqrt(rho) < (rho-1)/log rho < rho;
  6.  the grid cost rho/log(rho) is uniquely minimised at rho = e, C(4) = C(2),
      and C(2) < 1.07 e;
  7.  the Diophantine dichotomy:  the slack orbit of a geometric demand ladder
      alpha^n is dense in [1,2) iff log2(alpha) is irrational.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 0.  Numerically careful grid quantiser
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

EPS: float = 1e-12


def grid_ceil(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Smallest integer power of `rho` that is >= `x`.

    The naive `rho ** ceil(log(x, rho))` misfires when `x` is exactly a power of
    `rho`: floating point may return `log` a hair above the integer, and the
    quantiser then jumps a whole level, reporting a slack of `rho` instead of 1.
    We snap the logarithm to an integer when it is within EPS of one.
    """
    if rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("grid ratio must exceed 1")
    if x <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("request size must be positive")
    t: float = math.log(x) / math.log(rho)
    nearest: int = round(t)
    k: int = nearest if abs(t - nearest) < EPS else math.ceil(t)
    return float(rho) ** k


def slack(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Multiplicative overshoot gridCeil_rho(x) / x, always in [1, rho)."""
    return grid_ceil(rho, x) / x


def log_slack(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Overshoot measured in backoff levels; equals frac(-log_rho x)."""
    return math.log(slack(rho, x)) / math.log(rho)


def frac(t: float) -> float:
    """Fractional part t - floor(t)."""
    return t - math.floor(t)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1.  The photon-transport exchange
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TransportClass:
    """One traffic class: occupancy p in (0,1], demand d > 0, credit r."""
    name: str
    p: float
    d: float
    r: float


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Exchange:
    """A photon-transport exchange: constants beta, gamma, M and its classes."""
    beta: float
    gamma: float
    M: float
    classes: Tuple[TransportClass, ...]

    def gap(self, c: TransportClass) -> float:
        """Boltzmann cost of one successful transfer, corrected by credit."""
        g: float = self.beta * math.log(1.0 / c.p) + self.M + self.gamma - c.r
        if g <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError(f"class {c.name}: transport gap must be positive")
        return g

    def ideal(self, c: TransportClass) -> float:
        """The perfectly divisible fair share gamma * d / gap."""
        return self.gamma * c.d / self.gap(c)

    def service(self, c: TransportClass, rho: float = 2.0) -> float:
        """The window actually delivered by the grid-rho backoff arbiter."""
        return grid_ceil(rho, self.ideal(c))


def witness(x: float) -> Exchange:
    """Single-class exchange whose ideal share is exactly `x`.

    beta = gamma = M = 1, p = 1 (so log(1/p) = 0), r = 1, hence
    gap = 0 + 1 + 1 - 1 = 1 and ideal = gamma * x / 1 = x.
    """
    return Exchange(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, (TransportClass("w", 1.0, x, 1.0),))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 2.  Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def demo_floor_and_ceiling() -> None:
    rule("1. No starvation and the factor-two ceiling")
    ex = Exchange(
        beta=1.0,
        gamma=1.0,
        M=2.0,
        classes=(
            TransportClass("bulk",     p=0.90, d=3.0,  r=0.5),
            TransportClass("control",  p=0.60, d=1.0,  r=1.2),
            TransportClass("rare",     p=0.01, d=5.0,  r=0.0),
            TransportClass("priority", p=0.99, d=0.3,  r=2.4),
        ),
    )
    print(f"{'class':>10} {'p':>7} {'gap':>9} {'ideal':>11} {'service':>10} {'slack':>8}")
    for c in ex.classes:
        i, s = ex.ideal(c), ex.service(c)
        print(f"{c.name:>10} {c.p:7.2f} {ex.gap(c):9.4f} {i:11.6f} {s:10.5f} {s / i:8.5f}")
        assert i <= s + 1e-15,  "floor violated"
        assert s < 2.0 * i,     "ceiling violated"

    tot_i = sum(ex.ideal(c) for c in ex.classes)
    tot_s = sum(ex.service(c) for c in ex.classes)
    print(f"\naggregate:  sum(ideal) = {tot_i:.6f} <= sum(service) = {tot_s:.6f} "
          f"< 2*sum(ideal) = {2 * tot_i:.6f}")
    assert tot_i <= tot_s < 2.0 * tot_i
    print("The 'rare' class (p = 0.01) has a large Boltzmann cost and is squeezed")
    print("towards zero service: the floor is a saturating constraint, not a tautology.")


def demo_spectrum() -> None:
    rule("2. The slack spectrum is exactly [1, 2)")
    print("Target slack t is realised by the witness exchange with demand 2/t.\n")
    print(f"{'target t':>10} {'demand 2/t':>12} {'service':>9} {'realised':>10} {'error':>11}")
    targets: List[float] = [1.0, 1.05, 1.25, 1.4142135623730951, 1.5, 1.75, 1.9, 1.999]
    for t in targets:
        x = 2.0 / t
        ex = witness(x)
        c = ex.classes[0]
        realised = ex.service(c) / ex.ideal(c)
        print(f"{t:10.6f} {x:12.6f} {ex.service(c):9.4f} {realised:10.6f} "
              f"{abs(realised - t):11.2e}")
        assert abs(realised - t) < 1e-12

    print("\nA random sweep of ideal shares over 6 decades never leaves [1, 2):")
    lo, hi = 2.0, 1.0
    n = 20000
    for k in range(n):
        x = 10.0 ** (-3.0 + 6.0 * k / (n - 1))
        s = slack(2.0, x)
        lo, hi = min(lo, s), max(hi, s)
    print(f"  observed slack range over {n} samples: [{lo:.6f}, {hi:.6f}]")
    assert 1.0 <= lo and hi < 2.0


def demo_general_grid() -> None:
    rule("3. For grid ratio rho the optimal constants are 1 and rho")
    for rho in (1.5, 2.0, math.e, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0):
        lo, hi = math.inf, -math.inf
        n = 4000
        for k in range(n):
            x = rho ** (-3.0 + 6.0 * k / (n - 1)) * 1.0000001
            s = slack(rho, x)
            lo, hi = min(lo, s), max(hi, s)
        # the extreme witness: demand just above 1 forces the full jump to rho
        worst = slack(rho, 1.0 + 1e-9)
        print(f"  rho = {rho:6.4f}:  observed slack in [{lo:.6f}, {hi:.6f}], "
              f"near-worst witness slack = {worst:.6f} (sup = rho = {rho:.6f})")
        assert lo >= 1.0 - 1e-12 and hi < rho


def demo_jitter() -> None:
    rule("4. Jitter: worst case unchanged, typical case sqrt(rho), mean (rho-1)/log rho")

    def jitter_ceil(rho: float, theta: float, x: float) -> float:
        t = math.log(x) / math.log(rho) - theta
        nearest = round(t)
        k = nearest if abs(t - nearest) < EPS else math.ceil(t)
        return rho ** (k + theta)

    n_phase = 200000
    for rho in (2.0, math.e, 3.0, 4.0):
        x = 1.3719  # an arbitrary, generic request size
        worst = 0.0
        geo_log_sum = 0.0
        arith_sum = 0.0
        for j in range(n_phase):
            theta = (j + 0.5) / n_phase
            s = jitter_ceil(rho, theta, x) / x
            assert 1.0 <= s < rho + 1e-12, "phase-independent bound violated"
            worst = max(worst, s)
            geo_log_sum += math.log(s)
            arith_sum += s
        geo = math.exp(geo_log_sum / n_phase)
        ari = arith_sum / n_phase
        print(f"  rho = {rho:6.4f}:  sup over phases = {worst:.6f} (theory {rho:.6f});"
              f"  geometric mean = {geo:.6f} (theory {math.sqrt(rho):.6f});")
        print(f"{'':16}arithmetic mean = {ari:.6f} "
              f"(theory {(rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho):.6f})")
        assert abs(geo - math.sqrt(rho)) < 1e-4
        assert abs(ari - (rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho)) < 1e-4
        assert math.sqrt(rho) < (rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho) < rho

    print("\nRandomisation never lowers the supremum: the bound 1 <= slack < rho")
    print("holds at every single phase, so no phase law can beat it.")


def demo_grid_cost() -> None:
    rule("5. The grid cost rho/log(rho) is uniquely minimised at rho = e")

    def grid_cost(rho: float) -> float:
        return rho / math.log(rho)

    print(f"{'rho':>8} {'C(rho)':>12} {'excess over e':>16}")
    for rho in (1.5, 2.0, 2.5, math.e, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 8.0, 16.0):
        c = grid_cost(rho)
        print(f"{rho:8.4f} {c:12.6f} {100.0 * (c / math.e - 1.0):15.3f}%")
        assert c >= math.e - 1e-12

    print(f"\n  C(2) = {grid_cost(2.0):.9f}")
    print(f"  C(4) = {grid_cost(4.0):.9f}   (exactly equal to C(2))")
    print(f"  C(3) = {grid_cost(3.0):.9f}   (closest integer ratio to the optimum)")
    print(f"  e    = {math.e:.9f}")
    assert abs(grid_cost(4.0) - grid_cost(2.0)) < 1e-12
    assert grid_cost(2.0) < 1.07 * math.e

    # golden-section search recovers the optimum
    lo, hi = 1.2, 10.0
    inv_phi = (math.sqrt(5.0) - 1.0) / 2.0
    for _ in range(200):
        a = hi - inv_phi * (hi - lo)
        b = lo + inv_phi * (hi - lo)
        if grid_cost(a) < grid_cost(b):
            hi = b
        else:
            lo = a
    print(f"  golden-section minimiser: rho* = {(lo + hi) / 2:.12f}  (e = {math.e:.12f})")
    assert abs((lo + hi) / 2 - math.e) < 1e-6


def star_discrepancy(sample: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Exact star discrepancy of a finite sample of [0,1)."""
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    d = 0.0
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        d = max(d, abs((i + 1) / n - x), abs(i / n - x))
    return d


def demo_dichotomy() -> None:
    rule("6. Diophantine dichotomy: dense slack orbit iff log2(alpha) is irrational")
    print("Demand grows by a factor alpha per round; the ideal share climbs alpha^n")
    print("and the log-slack is frac(-n log2 alpha), an orbit of a circle rotation.\n")

    # Rational exponents are handled with exact fractions, so that the finite
    # orbit is reported exactly rather than being smeared by floating-point drift.
    rational_cases: List[Tuple[str, Fraction]] = [
        ("alpha = 4      (log2 alpha = 2)",     Fraction(2, 1)),
        ("alpha = sqrt2  (log2 alpha = 1/2)",   Fraction(1, 2)),
        ("alpha = 2**(3/7)",                    Fraction(3, 7)),
    ]
    irrational_cases: List[Tuple[str, float]] = [
        ("alpha = 3      (log2 3 irrational)",  3.0),
        ("alpha = 10     (log2 10 irrational)", 10.0),
        ("alpha = pi",                          math.pi),
    ]
    N = 4000
    header = (f"{'case':>36} {'#distinct':>10} {'discrepancy':>13} "
              f"{'min slack':>10} {'max slack':>10}")
    print(header)
    for label, theta in rational_cases:
        orbit_q = [(-n * theta) % 1 for n in range(N)]
        distinct = len(set(orbit_q))
        orbit = [float(v) for v in orbit_q]
        slacks = [2.0 ** v for v in orbit]
        print(f"{label:>36} {distinct:10d} {star_discrepancy(orbit):13.6f} "
              f"{min(slacks):10.6f} {max(slacks):10.6f}")
        assert distinct == theta.denominator, "orbit period must be the denominator"
    for label, alpha in irrational_cases:
        orbit = [frac(-n * math.log2(alpha)) for n in range(N)]
        distinct = len({round(v, 9) for v in orbit})
        disc = star_discrepancy(orbit)
        slacks = [2.0 ** v for v in orbit]
        print(f"{label:>36} {distinct:10d} {disc:13.6f} "
              f"{min(slacks):10.6f} {max(slacks):10.6f}")
        assert disc < 0.01, "irrational case must equidistribute"

    print("\nQuantitative saturation for ternary growth (alpha = 3), searching n >= 1:")
    theta3 = math.log2(3.0)
    horizon = 200000
    hi_n = max(range(1, horizon), key=lambda n: frac(-n * theta3))
    lo_n = min(range(1, horizon), key=lambda n: frac(-n * theta3))
    hi_s = 2.0 ** frac(-hi_n * theta3)
    lo_s = 2.0 ** frac(-lo_n * theta3)
    print(f"  best overshoot : n = {hi_n:6d}, slack = {hi_s:.9f}  (ceiling 2)")
    print(f"  best efficiency: m = {lo_n:6d}, slack = {lo_s:.9f}  (floor 1)")
    for eps in (0.5, 0.2, 0.05, 0.01):
        print(f"  eps = {eps:5.2f}:  {hi_s:.9f} > 2^(1-eps) = {2.0 ** (1 - eps):.6f}   and   "
              f"{lo_s:.9f} < 2^eps = {2.0 ** eps:.6f}")
        assert hi_s > 2.0 ** (1 - eps) and lo_s < 2.0 ** eps

    print("\nBy contrast, alpha = 4 has slack identically 1: perfect efficiency forever.")
    assert all(abs(slack(2.0, 4.0 ** n) - 1.0) < 1e-12 for n in range(-20, 21))


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__.strip().splitlines()[0])
    demos: Dict[str, Callable[[], None]] = {
        "floor/ceiling": demo_floor_and_ceiling,
        "spectrum": demo_spectrum,
        "general grid": demo_general_grid,
        "jitter": demo_jitter,
        "grid cost": demo_grid_cost,
        "dichotomy": demo_dichotomy,
    }
    for fn in demos.values():
        fn()
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print("All numerical checks passed.")
    print("=" * 74)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
",
    "demo_waiting": """"How long must an operator wait to see the worst case?

The slack spectrum of a backoff arbiter is exactly [1,2), and a single exchange whose
demand grows by a factor alpha per round realises a dense set of slacks precisely when
log2(alpha) is irrational.  This demo turns that qualitative statement into waiting
times: for each growth ratio it reports the first round whose overshoot exceeds a
prescribed threshold, and the first round whose overshoot is within a prescribed
tolerance of the perfect value 1.

It also verifies, for each ratio, that the observed extremes bracket the theoretical
ones, and shows the failure of the rational ratios to ever reach the ceiling.

Self-contained; standard library only.  Run:  python3 demo_waiting.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple


def frac(t: float) -> float:
    return t - math.floor(t)


def rational_exponent(alpha: float, max_den: int = 4096,
                      tol: float = 1e-12) -> Optional[Fraction]:
    """log2(alpha) as a fraction when it has a small one; else None."""
    x: float = math.log2(alpha)
    h_prev, h_cur, k_prev, k_cur = 0, 1, 1, 0
    b: float = x
    for _ in range(40):
        a: int = math.floor(b)
        h_next, k_next = a * h_cur + h_prev, a * k_cur + k_prev
        if k_next > max_den or k_next == 0:
            return None
        h_prev, h_cur, k_prev, k_cur = h_cur, h_next, k_cur, k_next
        if abs(x - h_cur / k_cur) < tol:
            return Fraction(h_cur, k_cur)
        rest: float = b - a
        if rest < 1e-14:
            return None
        b = 1.0 / rest
    return None


def log_slack(alpha: float, n: int, exponent: Optional[Fraction]) -> float:
    """The overshoot of round n in backoff levels, frac(-n log2 alpha).

    When log2(alpha) = p/q is rational the value is computed by exact modular
    arithmetic: floating-point drift would otherwise let a periodic orbit creep
    towards the ceiling it can never actually reach.
    """
    if exponent is not None:
        return ((-n * exponent.numerator) % exponent.denominator) / exponent.denominator
    return frac(-n * math.log2(alpha))


def first_round_above(alpha: float, threshold: float, horizon: int,
                      exponent: Optional[Fraction] = None) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest n >= 1 whose slack exceeds `threshold`."""
    goal = math.log2(threshold)
    for n in range(1, horizon):
        if log_slack(alpha, n, exponent) > goal:
            return n
    return None


def first_round_below(alpha: float, threshold: float, horizon: int,
                      exponent: Optional[Fraction] = None) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest n >= 1 whose slack is below `threshold`."""
    goal = math.log2(threshold)
    for n in range(1, horizon):
        if log_slack(alpha, n, exponent) < goal:
            return n
    return None


def main() -> None:
    horizon: int = 2 * 10 ** 6
    ratios: List[Tuple[str, float]] = [
        ("3 (ternary)", 3.0),
        ("10 (decimal)", 10.0),
        ("pi", math.pi),
        ("1.5", 1.5),
        ("4 (quaternary)", 4.0),
        ("sqrt 2", math.sqrt(2.0)),
        ("2^(3/7)", 2.0 ** (3 / 7)),
    ]
    thresholds: List[float] = [1.5, 1.9, 1.99, 1.999]

    print("Rounds until the overshoot first exceeds a given threshold")
    print("(a dash means: never, within the search horizon)\n")
    head = f"{'growth ratio':>16} {'log2 status':>16}"
    for t in thresholds:
        head += f" {'>' + format(t, '.3f'):>10}"
    head += f" {'within 1%':>11}"
    print(head)

    for label, alpha in ratios:
        q = rational_exponent(alpha)
        status = f"= {q}" if q is not None else "irrational"
        row = f"{label:>16} {status:>16}"
        search = horizon if q is None else 4 * q.denominator
        for t in thresholds:
            n = first_round_above(alpha, t, search, q)
            row += f" {(str(n) if n is not None else '—'):>10}"
        m = first_round_below(alpha, 1.01, search, q)
        row += f" {(str(m) if m is not None else '—'):>11}"
        print(row)
        if q is not None:
            # a rational exponent p/q gives at most q distinct overshoots
            values = {((-n * q.numerator) % q.denominator) / q.denominator
                      for n in range(4 * q.denominator)}
            assert len(values) == q.denominator
            top = 2.0 ** max(values)
            assert top <= 2.0 ** (1.0 - 1.0 / q.denominator) + 1e-12
        else:
            assert first_round_above(alpha, 1.99, horizon) is not None

    print("\nReading of the table:")
    print("  * irrational exponents reach every threshold, and the waiting time grows")
    print("    roughly like the reciprocal of the remaining gap to the ceiling 2;")
    print("  * alpha = 4 has overshoot identically 1: it never exceeds any threshold")
    print("    above 1, and it is within 1% of perfect on every single round;")
    print("  * alpha = sqrt(2) and alpha = 2^(3/7) cycle through 2 and 7 fixed values,")
    print("    so their maximum overshoot is capped strictly below 2 forever.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
",
    "algo_allocate": """"Grid-rho backoff allocation for a photon-transport exchange.

Given the global constants (beta, gamma, M) and, for each transport class, the
occupancy p, the demand d and the reservation credit r, this routine computes the
transport gap, the ideal (perfectly divisible) share and the window actually
delivered by a grid-rho backoff arbiter, together with the resulting overshoot.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

_LOG_SNAP: float = 1e-12


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TransportClass:
    """Occupancy p in (0,1], demand d > 0, reservation credit r."""
    name: str
    p: float
    d: float
    r: float


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Allocation:
    """The full allocation record of one class."""
    name: str
    gap: float
    ideal: float
    service: float
    slack: float


def grid_ceil(rho: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Least integer power of `rho` that is at least `x`.

    The logarithm is snapped to the nearest integer when it is within `_LOG_SNAP`
    of one; without this guard a share that sits exactly on the grid can be pushed
    to the next rung by floating-point error, inflating the reported overshoot
    from 1 all the way to rho.
    """
    if rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("grid ratio must exceed 1")
    if x <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("request size must be positive")
    t: float = math.log(x) / math.log(rho)
    nearest: int = round(t)
    k: int = nearest if abs(t - nearest) < _LOG_SNAP else math.ceil(t)
    return float(rho) ** k


def allocate(
    beta: float,
    gamma: float,
    M: float,
    classes: Sequence[TransportClass],
    rho: float = 2.0,
) -> List[Allocation]:
    """Allocate channel time to every class of an exchange.

    Raises ValueError if a class has a non-positive transport gap, which is the
    admissibility condition of the model.
    """
    if beta <= 0.0 or gamma <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("beta and gamma must be positive")
    out: List[Allocation] = []
    for c in classes:
        if not (0.0 < c.p <= 1.0):
            raise ValueError(f"{c.name}: occupancy must lie in (0,1]")
        if c.d <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError(f"{c.name}: demand must be positive")
        gap: float = beta * math.log(1.0 / c.p) + M + gamma - c.r
        if gap <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError(f"{c.name}: transport gap must be positive")
        ideal: float = gamma * c.d / gap
        service: float = grid_ceil(rho, ideal)
        out.append(Allocation(c.name, gap, ideal, service, service / ideal))
    return out


def audit(allocations: Sequence[Allocation], rho: float = 2.0) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Check the guarantee and summarise the aggregate cost of quantisation."""
    for a in allocations:
        assert a.ideal <= a.service * (1.0 + 1e-15), f"{a.name}: floor violated"
        assert a.service < rho * a.ideal, f"{a.name}: ceiling violated"
    tot_ideal: float = sum(a.ideal for a in allocations)
    tot_service: float = sum(a.service for a in allocations)
    return {
        "total_ideal": tot_ideal,
        "total_service": tot_service,
        "aggregate_slack": tot_service / tot_ideal,
        "max_slack": max(a.slack for a in allocations),
        "min_slack": min(a.slack for a in allocations),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo: Tuple[TransportClass, ...] = (
        TransportClass("bulk", 0.90, 3.0, 0.5),
        TransportClass("control", 0.60, 1.0, 1.2),
        TransportClass("rare", 0.01, 5.0, 0.0),
        TransportClass("priority", 0.99, 0.3, 2.4),
    )
    allocs = allocate(beta=1.0, gamma=1.0, M=2.0, classes=demo, rho=2.0)
    for a in allocs:

",
    "algo_orbit": """"Slack-orbit sampler and the Diophantine classifier for a growing exchange.

A class whose demand grows by a factor alpha each round has ideal share alpha^n,
and the overshoot of the dyadic arbiter, measured in backoff levels, is exactly
frac(-n * log2(alpha)) -- the orbit of a rotation of the circle R/Z.  The orbit is
dense (so the exchange eventually realises every slack in [1,2)) precisely when
log2(alpha) is irrational; if log2(alpha) = p/q in lowest terms the orbit is
periodic with period q and only q overshoot values ever occur.

This module samples the orbit, measures its star discrepancy, and classifies the
growth ratio via continued fractions.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple


def frac(t: float) -> float:
    """Fractional part t - floor(t)."""
    return t - math.floor(t)


def star_discrepancy(sample: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Exact star discrepancy sup_a |#{x_i < a}/N - a| of a sample of [0,1)."""
    xs: List[float] = sorted(sample)
    n: int = len(xs)
    d: float = 0.0
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        d = max(d, abs((i + 1) / n - x), abs(i / n - x))
    return d


def rational_exponent(alpha: float, max_den: int = 4096,
                      tol: float = 1e-12) -> Optional[Fraction]:
    """Return log2(alpha) as a fraction if it has one with denominator <= max_den.

    Continued-fraction expansion; a convergent p/q of an irrational number misses
    by at least about 1/q^2, so a hit within `tol` with q <= max_den is decisive
    evidence of rationality at this precision.
    """
    x: float = math.log2(alpha)
    h_prev, h_cur = 0, 1
    k_prev, k_cur = 1, 0
    b: float = x
    for _ in range(40):
        a: int = math.floor(b)
        h_next, k_next = a * h_cur + h_prev, a * k_cur + k_prev
        if k_next > max_den or k_next == 0:
            return None
        h_prev, h_cur = h_cur, h_next
        k_prev, k_cur = k_cur, k_next
        if abs(x - h_cur / k_cur) < tol:
            return Fraction(h_cur, k_cur)
        rest: float = b - a
        if rest < 1e-14:
            return None
        b = 1.0 / rest
    return None


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OrbitReport:
    alpha: float
    rounds: int
    exponent: Optional[Fraction]
    dense: bool
    distinct: int
    discrepancy: float
    min_slack: float
    max_slack: float
    geometric_mean: float
    arithmetic_mean: float


def sample_orbit(alpha: float, rounds: int) -> List[float]:
    """The log-slacks frac(-n log2 alpha) for n = 0 .. rounds-1.

    In the rational case exact modular arithmetic is used, so the finite orbit is
    reported exactly rather than being smeared by floating-point drift.
    """
    if alpha <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("growth ratio must be positive")
    q = rational_exponent(alpha)
    if q is not None:
        p_num, q_den = q.numerator, q.denominator
        return [((-n * p_num) % q_den) / q_den for n in range(rounds)]
    theta: float = math.log2(alpha)
    return [frac(-n * theta) for n in range(rounds)]


def analyse(alpha: float, rounds: int = 4000) -> OrbitReport:
    """Sample the orbit and summarise its equidistribution behaviour."""
    orbit: List[float] = sample_orbit(alpha, rounds)
    slacks: List[float] = [2.0 ** u for u in orbit]
    exponent = rational_exponent(alpha)
    return OrbitReport(
        alpha=alpha,
        rounds=rounds,
        exponent=exponent,
        dense=exponent is None,
        distinct=len({round(u, 9) for u in orbit}),
        discrepancy=star_discrepancy(orbit),
        min_slack=min(slacks),
        max_slack=max(slacks),
        geometric_mean=math.exp(sum(math.log(s) for s in slacks) / rounds),
        arithmetic_mean=sum(slacks) / rounds,
    )


def first_round_exceeding(alpha: float, target: float,
                          horizon: int = 10 ** 6) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest n >= 1 whose slack exceeds `target` (in [1,2)), or None."""
    if not 1.0 <= target < 2.0:
        raise ValueError("target slack must lie in [1,2)")
    theta: float = math.log2(alpha)
    goal: float = math.log2(target)
    for n in range(1, horizon):
        if frac(-n * theta) > goal:
            return n
    return None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for a in (4.0, math.sqrt(2.0), 2.0 ** (3 / 7), 3.0, math.pi, 10.0):
        rep = analyse(a)
        kind = "dense" if rep.dense else f"periodic, log2 = {rep.exponent}"
        print(f"alpha = {a:8.5f}  {kind:>26}  distinct={rep.distinct:5d}  "
              f"D*={rep.discrepancy:.6f}  slack in "
              f"[{rep.min_slack:.6f}, {rep.max_slack:.6f}]")
    print("first ternary round with slack > 1.99:",
          first_round_exceeding(3.0, 1.99))
",
    "algo_gridcost": """"Optimisation of the backoff grid ratio.

The worst-case overshoot of a grid-rho arbiter is rho, and one backoff level covers
log(rho) of logarithmic dynamic range, so the natural figure of merit is the grid
cost C(rho) = rho / log(rho).  Since C'(rho) = (log rho - 1)/(log rho)^2, the unique
stationary point is rho = e, C is strictly decreasing on (1,e) and strictly
increasing on (e, infinity), and C(e) = e is the global minimum.

This module provides the analytic constants, a derivative-free golden-section
search that recovers the optimum numerically, and a report of the three slack
constants attached to a candidate ratio.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


def grid_cost(rho: float) -> float:
    """C(rho) = rho / log(rho), defined for rho > 1."""
    if rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("grid ratio must exceed 1")
    return rho / math.log(rho)


def typical_slack(rho: float) -> float:
    """Geometric-mean overshoot of the phase-jittered grid-rho arbiter: sqrt(rho)."""
    return math.sqrt(rho)


def mean_slack(rho: float) -> float:
    """Arithmetic-mean overshoot of the jittered arbiter: (rho - 1)/log(rho)."""
    return (rho - 1.0) / math.log(rho)


def worst_case_slack(rho: float) -> float:
    """Supremum of the overshoot, approached but never attained: rho."""
    return rho


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GridReport:
    rho: float
    typical: float
    mean: float
    worst: float
    cost: float
    excess_over_optimum: float


def report(rho: float) -> GridReport:
    """All four constants of a candidate grid ratio, plus its relative excess."""
    c = grid_cost(rho)
    return GridReport(
        rho=rho,
        typical=typical_slack(rho),
        mean=mean_slack(rho),
        worst=worst_case_slack(rho),
        cost=c,
        excess_over_optimum=c / math.e - 1.0,
    )


def golden_section_min(f: Callable[[float], float], lo: float, hi: float,
                       iterations: int = 200) -> float:
    """Minimise a strictly unimodal f on [lo, hi]; O(iterations) evaluations."""
    inv_phi: float = (math.sqrt(5.0) - 1.0) / 2.0
    for _ in range(iterations):
        a = hi - inv_phi * (hi - lo)
        b = lo + inv_phi * (hi - lo)
        if f(a) < f(b):
            hi = b
        else:
            lo = a
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def optimal_ratio(lo: float = 1.2, hi: float = 10.0) -> float:
    """Numerically recover the unique minimiser of the grid cost (equal to e)."""
    return golden_section_min(grid_cost, lo, hi)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    candidates: List[float] = [1.5, 2.0, 2.5, math.e, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 8.0]
    print(f"{'rho':>8} {'typical':>10} {'mean':>10} {'worst':>8} "
          f"{'C(rho)':>10} {'excess':>9}")
    for rho in candidates:
        r = report(rho)
        print(f"{r.rho:8.5f} {r.typical:10.5f} {r.mean:10.5f} {r.worst:8.4f} "
              f"{r.cost:10.6f} {100 * r.excess_over_optimum:8.3f}%")
        assert r.typical < r.mean < r.worst, "the three constants must be ordered"
        assert r.cost >= math.e - 1e-12, "e is a lower bound for the grid cost"

    pairs: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [(2.0, 4.0)]
    for a, b in pairs:
        print(f"\nC({a}) = {grid_cost(a):.12f} = C({b}) = {grid_cost(b):.12f}")
        assert abs(grid_cost(a) - grid_cost(b)) < 1e-12

    rho_star = optimal_ratio()
    print(f"golden-section optimum: {rho_star:.12f}  (e = {math.e:.12f})")
    print(f"dyadic excess over the optimum: "
          f"{100 * report(2.0).excess_over_optimum:.3f}%  (< 7%)")
",
    "viz_sawtooth": """"Visualisation: the log-periodic slack sawtooth and two demand ladders.

Panel (a) draws the multiplicative overshoot  slack(x) = 2^{frac(-log2 x)}  of the
dyadic backoff arbiter against log2 of the request size.  The curve is a sawtooth
of period 1: it drops to the floor 1 exactly on the grid x = 2^k and climbs back
towards -- but never reaches -- the ceiling 2.

Panel (b) overlays the demand ladders of two exchanges on that sawtooth.  A class
whose demand grows by a factor 3 per round samples the sawtooth at the points
frac(-n log2 3), which equidistribute; a class growing by a factor 4 per round
lands on the grid every time and has slack identically 1.

Panel (c) shows the empirical distribution of the slack for the ternary ladder
after 20000 rounds: the density of 2^U for U uniform on [0,1], i.e. the density
1/(s log 2) on [1,2).

Requires: matplotlib, numpy.  Run:  python3 viz_sawtooth.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def frac(t: float) -> float:
    return t - math.floor(t)


def slack_from_log(u: float) -> float:
    """Slack as a function of u = log2(request size)."""
    return 2.0 ** frac(-u)


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 12))

    # ---- panel (a): the sawtooth ------------------------------------------ #
    us = np.linspace(-3.0, 3.0, 20001)
    ss = np.array([slack_from_log(u) for u in us])
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.plot(us, ss, lw=1.6, color="#1f4e79")
    ax.axhline(1.0, color="#2e7d32", ls="--", lw=1.2, label="floor 1 (attained)")
    ax.axhline(2.0, color="#c62828", ls="--", lw=1.2, label="ceiling 2 (never attained)")
    for k in range(-3, 4):
        ax.plot([k], [1.0], "o", color="#2e7d32", ms=5)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\log_2$ (request size)")
    ax.set_ylabel("slack  service / ideal")
    ax.set_title("(a) The slack is log-periodic with period 1: range exactly [1, 2)")
    ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.15)
    ax.legend(loc="center right")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

    # ---- panel (b): two demand ladders ------------------------------------ #
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.plot(us, ss, lw=1.0, color="#bbbbbb")
    n_max = 40
    tern_u: List[float] = [(n * math.log2(3.0)) % 1 for n in range(n_max)]
    quad_u: List[float] = [(n * math.log2(4.0)) % 1 for n in range(n_max)]
    ax.plot(tern_u, [slack_from_log(u) for u in tern_u], "o",
            color="#8e24aa", ms=6, label=r"ternary growth $\alpha=3$ ($\log_2 3$ irrational)")
    ax.plot(quad_u, [slack_from_log(u) for u in quad_u], "s",
            color="#ef6c00", ms=11, zorder=5, mec="black",
            label=r"quaternary growth $\alpha=4$ ($\log_2 4 = 2$): slack $\equiv 1$")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.05, 1.05)
    ax.set_ylim(0.92, 2.18)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\log_2$ (request size)  mod  1")
    ax.set_ylabel("slack")
    ax.set_title("(b) One exchange, watched over time: dense orbit versus a single point")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

    # ---- panel (c): the limiting slack distribution ----------------------- #
    ax = axes[2]
    n_hist = 20000
    vals = np.array([2.0 ** frac(-n * math.log2(3.0)) for n in range(n_hist)])
    ax.hist(vals, bins=80, density=True, color="#8e24aa", alpha=0.55,
            label=f"ternary ladder, {n_hist} rounds")
    grid = np.linspace(1.0, 2.0, 400)
    ax.plot(grid, 1.0 / (grid * math.log(2.0)), lw=2.0, color="#1f4e79",
            label=r"limiting density $1/(s\log 2)$ on $[1,2)$")
    ax.axvline(math.sqrt(2.0), color="#2e7d32", ls="--",
               label=r"geometric mean $\sqrt{2}\approx1.4142$")
    ax.axvline(1.0 / math.log(2.0), color="#c62828", ls=":",
               label=r"arithmetic mean $1/\log 2\approx1.4427$")
    ax.set_xlabel("slack")
    ax.set_ylabel("density")
    ax.set_title("(c) The empirical slack distribution and the two mean constants")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("slack_sawtooth.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote slack_sawtooth.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

concept.title: Persistent Homology of Prime Numbers: The Topology of Arithmetic
concept.concept_description: The sequence of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ... defines a point cloud in R where the n-th prime p_n is at position p_n on the real line. The gaps between primes create a topological structure. Define the persistent homology of the prime point cloud as the Rips filtration R_epsilon = {p_n : |p_m - p_n| <= epsilon}. As epsilon increases, more primes are connected, and the topology changes. Conjecture: The persistent H_0 (connected components) of the prime point cloud has the same barcode as a Poisson point process with intensity 1/log(x). Specifically, the bar lengths in H_0 follow an exponential distribution with mean equal to the average prime gap (which is approximately log(x) by the prime number theorem). The persistent H_1 (1-dimensional holes) of the prime point cloud appears at scale epsilon ~ log(x)^2, corresponding to prime pairs (p, p+2k) where 2k is a specific even gap. The longest H_1 bar corresponds to the twin prime conjecture: it persists from epsilon = 2 (the twin prime scale) to epsilon = infinity. Test: compute persistent homology of the primes up to 10^6 using Rips filtration and compare with the Poisson point process prediction. Verify that H_0 bar lengths are exponentially distributed with mean log(x). Impact: primes have topology — their gaps create persistent homology that encodes the twin prime conjecture and other arithmetic properties.

**Domain**: NumberTheory

Specifically, the bar lengths in H_0 follow an exponential distribution with mean equal to the average prime gap (which is approximately log(x) by the prime number theorem). The persistent H_1 (1-dimensional holes) of the prime point cloud appears at scale epsilon ~ log(x)^2, corresponding to prime pairs (p, p+2k) where 2k is a specific even gap. The longest H_1 bar corresponds to the twin prime conjecture: it persists from epsilon = 2 (the twin prime scale) to epsilon = infinity. Test: compute persistent homology of the primes up to 10^6 using Rips filtration and compare with the Poisson point process prediction. /-! ### The bar-length spectrum is atomic -/

/-- The first `H₀` bar of the prime cloud, from `2` to `3`, has length `1`. -/
theorem primeGap_zero : TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap 0 = 1 := by
  unfold TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap
  simp

/-- Every prime after the first is odd. -/
theorem nth_prime_odd {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) : Odd (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) := by
  have h3 : (3 : ℕ) ≤ Nat.nth Nat.Prime n := by
    have : Nat.nth Nat.Prime 1 ≤ Nat.nth Nat.Prime n :=
      Nat.nth_monotone Nat.infinite_setOf_prime hn
    simpa using this
  have hp : (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n).Prime := Nat.prime_nth_prime n
  rcases hp.eq_two_or_odd' with h | h
  · omega
  · exact h

/-- Bars are strictly positive: consecutive primes are distinct. -/
theorem primeGap_pos (n : ℕ) : 0 < TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap n := by
  have h : Nat.nth Nat.Prime n < Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1) :=
    Nat.nth_strictMono Nat.infinite_setOf_prime (Nat.lt_succ_self n)
  unfold TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap
  omega

/-- All bars after the first have even length. -/
theorem primeGap_even {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) : Even (TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap n) := by
  have ha : Nat.nth Nat.Prime n % 2 = 1 := Nat.odd_iff.mp (nth_prime_odd hn)
  have hb : Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1) % 2 = 1 :=
    Nat.odd_iff.mp (nth_prime_odd (le_trans hn (Nat.le_succ n)))
  have h : Nat.nth Nat.Prime n < Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1) :=
    Nat.nth_strictMono Nat.infinite_setOf_prime (Nat.lt_succ_self n)
  rw [Nat.even_iff]
  unfold TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap
  omega

/-- **The bar-length spectrum of the prime barcode is atomic.**  Every bar has length `1`
(and this happens only for the very first bar) or an even length `≥ 2`. -/
theorem barLength_lattice (n : ℕ) :
    (n = 0 ∧ TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap n = 1) ∨
      (1 ≤ n ∧ Even (TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap n) ∧ 2 ≤ TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap n) := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos n with rfl | hn
  · exact Or.inl ⟨rfl, primeGap_zero⟩
  · refine Or.inr ⟨hn, primeGap_even hn, ?_⟩
    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := primeGap_even hn
    have := primeGap_pos n
    omega

/-- Only the very first bar is shorter than `2`. -/
theorem short_bar_iff (i : ℕ) : ((TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap i : ℝ) < 2) ↔ i = 0 := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    by_contra hi
    have hi' : 1 ≤ i := Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.mpr hi
    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := primeGap_even hi'
    have hpos := primeGap_pos i
    have h2 : (2 : ℕ) ≤ TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap i := by omega
    have : ((2 : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap i : ℝ) := Nat.cast_le.mpr h2
    push_cast at this
    linarith
  · rintro rfl
    rw [primeGap_zero]
    norm_num

/-- **Exactly one short bar.**  Among the first `n ≥ 1` bars of the prime barcode there is
exactly one of length `< 2`. -/
theorem card_short_bars_eq_one {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i => (TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap i : ℝ) < 2)).card = 1 := by
  classical
  have : (Finset.range n).filter (fun i => (TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap i : ℝ) < 2) = {0} := by
    ext i
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range, Finset.mem_singleton]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨-, h⟩
      exact (short_bar_iff i).mp h
    · rintro rfl
      exact ⟨hn, (short_bar_iff 0).mpr rfl⟩
  rw [this]
  simp

first `n`, a quantity tending to infinity, whereas the prime barcode has exactly one such
bar.  Consequently no exponential law — with mean `log x` or with any other mean — can
describe the `H₀` bar lengths of the primes. -/

total persistence and the Betti staircase `b₀(ε, n) = 1 + #{i < n : gap_i > ε}`.  The
research mission then conjectured that this barcode is statistically indistinguishable from
that of a Poisson point process of intensity `1/log x`: the bar lengths should be
*exponentially distributed* with mean `≈ log x`.

This file tests that conjecture and **refutes it**, and then converts the surviving
arithmetic content into topology.

* `PrimeBarcodeArith.barLength_lattice` — the bar-length spectrum is *atomic*: every `H₀`
  bar of the prime cloud has length `1` (the single bar `2 ↦ 3`) or an even length `≥ 2`.
  A continuous exponential law is therefore impossible.

* `PrimeBarcodeArith.card_short_bars_eq_one` — quantitatively, the number of bars of length
  `< 2` among the first `n` bars is **exactly one**, for every `n ≥ 1`.

* `PrimeBarcodeArith.poisson_short_bar_prediction_fails` — the refutation: for *every*

  whatsoever (in particular with mean `log x`), fits the prime `H₀` barcode.

  is a Betti defect**: for `n ≥ 1`, `b₀(2, n) + #{i < n : gap_i = 2} = n`.

* `PrimeBarcodeArith.twinPrime_iff_bettiDefect_unbounded` — the **twin prime conjecture** is

  cloud at scale `2`.

  and hence `PrimeBarcodeArith.bettiZero_unbounded`: at *every fixed scale* the prime cloud
  breaks into arbitrarily many connected components.

  `δ`-perturbation of a line cloud shifts its Betti curve by at most `2δ` in scale.  In
  particular the prime barcode is robust: it is not an artefact of the exact positions of
